RUNNING FOR Mayor of Toronto — ELECTION DAY Mon, Oct 26, 2026
doc_title: Brad Bradford for Mayor of Toronto | A City We Can Be Proud Of

text:
Torontonians give their time, their talent, and their taxes to this city every single day. They deserve a mayor who finally gives that back.

Brad Bradford loves this city. An urban planner, City Councillor, husband, and dad of two, Brad has spent his career on the work of how cities actually get built and how City Hall actually works. He believes Toronto can be the best city in the world to raise a family, build a business, and unlock your potential. That belief is what got him into public service, and it is what gets him out of bed every morning.

text: Brad is running for Mayor because Torontonians have been taught to accept less, and he refuses to. He believes we deserve a city we can be proud of again, one that works for the people who pay for it. His campaign is focused on the three things Torontonians struggle with every day: Crime, Congestion, and Cost.

Brad will take his seat on the Toronto Police Service Board that is reserved for the mayor, and hire 1,000 new front-line police officers over his first term. A city that is not safe is not free. He will also crack down on dangerous e-bikes and increase voluntary and mandatory treatment options for people struggling with serious addiction. He will judge success by one test: whether residents in every part of the city feel safe on their streets, on transit and in their homes.

text:
TORONTO, ON | This morning in the Upper Beach, Brad Bradford sat down with a group of Toronto mothers for a kitchen-table conversation about the things that keep them up at night: the cost of staying in this city, whether the playground is safe, the hours lost in traffic that should be spent with their kids, and whether their children will ever be able to afford a home of their own here.

"Every mom at that table is doing everything right. Working, saving, driving the carpool, checking the wood chips for needles before the kids get off the slide," said Bradford. "They're holding this city together, and every year they pay more and get less for it. Toronto isn't broken. It's stuck. And the families holding it together are the ones paying the price."
doc_title: Bradford to Toronto moms: This should be the best city in the world to raise a family. Right now, it doesn't feel like it

text:
The province has never given the City of Toronto more money than it has over the past 3 years. NDP Mayor Chow still raised property taxes nearly 20%, the largest increase in the city's history. If she's re-elected she'll raise them another 20% at least. In the same 3 years, food bank visits climbed to 4.1 million a year, up 340% since 2019. More than 1 in 10 of our neighbours now needs a food bank to get through the month, and plenty of them are parents. Where did the money go?

Bradford heard the same story from mothers around the table that he has heard at doors across the city. A family buys a condo to get a foot in the door. Then the second child arrives, and they need more space. Toronto is the only city in Canada that charges its own land transfer tax on top of the province's, so moving up in this city means handing City Hall tens of thousands of dollars in cash on closing day, on top of the down payment, the lawyer and the moving truck. Many families look at that bill and move out of Toronto altogether. The city loses them, their kids leave their schools and their friends, and the grandparents are an hour away.
doc_title: Bradford to Toronto moms: This should be the best city in the world to raise a family. Right now, it doesn't feel like it

text: "The double land transfer tax is a tax on growing up and a tax on growing your family," said Bradford. "As mayor, I'll eliminate Toronto's municipal land transfer tax on the value of a home below the average Toronto price, $1.1 million. That's for first-time buyers, and it's for the family that already lives here and needs a bigger place when the kids arrive. At the threshold, that's about $18,000 back. No family should have to leave the city they love because City Hall made it too expensive to stay."
doc_title: Bradford to Toronto moms: This should be the best city in the world to raise a family. Right now, it doesn't feel like it

text:
Safety came up at every turn. Mothers described walking the playground before letting their kids play. Planning the route to school around the corners to avoid. Another weekend, another shooting on the news. As mayor, Bradford will take his seat on the Toronto Police Services Board, put 1,000 more front line officers on the street and a visible police presence at every subway station, go after the repeat violent offenders who are terrorizing the same neighbourhoods over and over, install platform edge doors on the subway, and bring in more voluntary and, in severe cases, mandatory treatment for people whose addiction has taken over their lives, so that parks and playgrounds belong to families again.

"A city that is not safe is not free," said Bradford. "A mom should not have to do a sweep of the sandbox before her four year old can play in it. Compassion for people struggling with addiction and safe public spaces for children are not opposites. A real city delivers both."
doc_title: Bradford to Toronto moms: This should be the best city in the world to raise a family. Right now, it doesn't feel like it

text:
Then there is the time. Toronto has the worst commutes in North America, and nobody voted for that. For a working parent it means missing dinner, missing the game, missing bedtime. Bradford calls it the time tax: hours you never get back, and nobody at City Hall can tell you where they went. His plan includes a 15 minute service guarantee on the TTC and a single point of accountability for construction across the city, with published timelines and consequences when they slip.

Bradford's plan for families starts with affordability: a property tax freeze in year one, water bills cut 25%, about $300 a year for the average household, keeping Toronto's school food program so every kid is fed, and fixing the recreation registration system so parents aren't racing a crashing website at 7 in the morning for a swimming spot. All of it backed by the first full, independent, line by line review of City spending since 2011, so every dollar is accounted for before anyone at City Hall asks a family for another one.
doc_title: Bradford to Toronto moms: This should be the best city in the world to raise a family. Right now, it doesn't feel like it

text:
NDP Mayor Chow stood on the debate stage and declared that Toronto has reached its full potential. Bradford rejects that. In a city where 4.1 million food bank visits a year is normal, where parents check playgrounds for needles and families move away because they can't afford to grow, we're not even close.

"I want Toronto to be the best city in the world to raise a family. Not someday. Now," said Bradford. "The moms I met this morning haven't given up on this city, and neither have I. We're on the cusp of change. Change is within our grasp. But to change the city, we need to change the mayor. On October 26, Toronto's families can choose a city they can afford, a city that moves, and a city that feels safe. A Toronto we can be proud of again."

text: TORONTO, ON | Brad Bradford today set out how a Bradford administration will modernize the way Toronto budgets, the way the federal government did 30 years ago and the Ontario government did 20 years ago. Toronto has the eighth-largest government budget in Canada, larger than four provinces, and still keeps its books the way it did in the 1990s.
doc_title: Bradford presents new fiscal framework to modernize Toronto's budget

text: City Hall says its operating and capital budgets are separate. On paper, they are. In practice, hundreds of millions of dollars a year are moved out of the operating budget, funded by that year’s property taxes and land transfer tax, to pre-pay for capital projects that taxpayers won’t use for years. The City’s own 2026 Budget already earmarks about $256 million of those transfers for 2027 and about $369 million for 2028. Ending this cross-subsidy will allow Bradford to deliver on his transformational commitments to eliminate the Municipal Land Transfer Tax for the average homebuyer while maintaining capital investments, with no service cuts. Last year, more than $1 billion of the capital budget went unspent, meaning important projects the city committed to building were not delivered. That is one reason why property taxes go up every year for infrastructure that residents don’t get to use and the pipes, community centres and transit stations still wait.
doc_title: Bradford presents new fiscal framework to modernize Toronto's budget

text:
“Everyone at City Hall agrees Toronto has a structural budget problem. NDP Mayor Chow was elected to fix it. She started with a $1.7 billion hole, left over from the pandemic. Three years and nearly 20% in tax increases later, she is leaving a $1.6 billion hole for next year. She didn’t fix the problem. She just sent you the bill,” said Brad Bradford, candidate for Mayor of Toronto. “The problem was never that Toronto is poor. The problem is a budget rulebook from the 1990s that overtaxes people today to pay cash for things that don’t get built. Residents are done with Mayor Chow overtaxing, misspending, and underbuilding. I’m going to change the rulebook and modernize the budget.”

For eight years, through a pandemic that blew a hole in every big-city budget in the country, Toronto kept property tax increases at or below inflation. It took discipline every single year, because the rulebook never made it easy. In 2023 the discipline left the building. "Holding the line shouldn't depend on who's sitting in the chair," said Bradford.
doc_title: Bradford presents new fiscal framework to modernize Toronto's budget

text:
"Our Prime Minister has modernized our country’s books, with separate operating and capital budgets. Truly embracing the same practices here gives Toronto a modern, sustainable budget that protects services today and lets us invest more in transit, roads and community centres."

Bradford’s plan to modernize the budget

-
A real separation of the operating and capital budgets. The operating budget, which runs the city, is paid for by taxes and fees and balances every year. The capital budget, which builds the city, is financed over the life of each asset, the way a family pays for a home.

-
End the cross subsidy. No more shipping hundreds of millions of dollars a year from the operating budget to pre-pay the capital budget, which Mayor Chow doesn’t actually deliver on. That money goes back to the people who paid it by eliminating the double land transfer tax on the value of a principal home below the average Toronto price.
doc_title: Bradford presents new fiscal framework to modernize Toronto's budget

text:
-
The tightest debt rules in the country. Debt interest never above 4 cents of every revenue dollar, lower than any province, Chicago, New York or Montreal. Total debt costs never above 10% of own-source revenue. Borrowing for building in the capital budget only, never for operating expenses.

-
A year one property tax freeze. The first full, independent, line by line review of City spending since 2011, before anyone at City Hall asks taxpayers for another dollar. After the first year, property taxes grow below inflation. Frontline service cuts are off the table.

-
A better way to build and fund infrastructure. Reduce water bills by $300 a year for residents. Establish Toronto Water as a 100% municipally-owned utility and find savings from the 67% of the budget that currently goes towards capital reserves.
doc_title: Bradford presents new fiscal framework to modernize Toronto's budget

text:
Nothing here is untested. Ottawa modernized its books in the 1990s to stop pre-financing infrastructure and in its most recent budget drew a clear line between what it spends to run the country and what it invests to build it. Queen’s Park made the same change two decades ago. Toronto Hydro has financed 100-year assets this way since 1999. Toronto is the outlier among major governments.

The choice on October 26

The province has never sent the City more money. NDP Mayor Chow still raised property taxes nearly 20%, starting with 9.5%, the largest increase in the city’s history. If she’s re-elected, she’ll raise them another 20% at least. Food bank visits are up 340% since 2019, 4.1 million last year alone. Olivia Chow stood on the debate stage and declared that Toronto has reached its full potential.
doc_title: Bradford presents new fiscal framework to modernize Toronto's budget

text:
“That’s the choice. The status quo, another 20% on your property taxes, and a hole in the budget that never gets smaller. Or we do it a different way, the way every other government in this country the size of Toronto already does it, and break the cycle of overtaxing and underbuilding,” said Bradford. “Toronto isn’t broken. It’s stuck. We’re on the cusp of change. Change is within our grasp. To change the city, we need to change the mayor.”

TORONTO, ON | This morning at the offices of Borrowell, a Toronto-founded fintech company, Brad Bradford sat down with CEO Andrew Graham and a group of students and young professionals to talk about what it takes to start a career, buy a first home and build a life in Toronto. They were joined by the President & CEO of Youth Employment Services (YES), Timothy Lang. Their conclusion is that the city is making it harder than it should be at every step.

Youth unemployment in Toronto is at 17%, four points higher than the national average. Across the country, the share of young people holding a job fell last year to its lowest level since 1998. Toronto's own Youth Cabinet found that 74% of young people face real barriers to employment. Add record rents, a land transfer tax no other Canadian city charges, and the worst commutes in North America, and the result is a generation doing the math on whether to stay or leave.
doc_title: BRADFORD SHARES PLAN TO RESTORE THE PROMISE OF TORONTO FOR TORONTO’S YOUTH

text:
"Toronto has Canada's biggest tech hub and the country's largest financial centre in the same few square kilometres. Almost no city in the world has both," said Bradford. "We should be competing with New York, London and Singapore for every ambitious 24-year-old on the continent. Instead we're driving our own out. Not because they stopped loving Toronto. Because they stopped believing it's a place where they can build a good life. I won't accept that."

Bradford's plan to create opportunity for Toronto youth has 4 parts. As mayor, he will:
doc_title: BRADFORD SHARES PLAN TO RESTORE THE PROMISE OF TORONTO FOR TORONTO’S YOUTH

text:
-
Launch the Toronto Youth Employment Challenge: a direct challenge from the Mayor's office to Toronto's employers to create 15,000 permanent, full-time youth jobs by the end of his term, 5,000 in year one. Bradford will personally recruit 10 to 15 CEOs as founding Anchor Partners, publish every pledge on a public portal with a quarterly leaderboard, and reserve 30% of placements for young people facing the steepest barriers. Employers fund the jobs. The City funds only the coordination, at under $750,000 a year. Boston's mayor delivered more than 10,500 youth hires in 2025 this way, and New York's CEOs have hired more than 65,000 young people since 2021.

-
Eliminate the municipal land transfer tax on the value of a home below the average Toronto price, $1.1 million. Under Bradford's plan, up to two thirds of homes sold in Toronto change hands with no city land transfer tax, about $18,000 back at the threshold. Most first-time buyers purchase condos, so for most of them the tax disappears entirely. It's funded with money the City already collects, and not one service is cut.
doc_title: BRADFORD SHARES PLAN TO RESTORE THE PROMISE OF TORONTO FOR TORONTO’S YOUTH

text:
-
Clean up the city and make it safe, starting at Union Station, the front door of the country: a police station inside Union and another at Yonge-Dundas, published cleaning and safety standards, a visible police presence at every subway station, 1,000 more front line officers, and real help for people in a mental health crisis, including more voluntary and mandatory treatment options for people whose addiction has taken over their lives.

-
Build a City Hall that competes: a 15 minute transit service guarantee, a single point of accountability for construction with published timelines, faster permitting, and the first full, independent, line by line review of City spending since 2011.

"The CEO deciding where to locate the next 200 jobs isn't asking about our tax incentives. The question is whether her people can get to work easily, afford a home and feel safe walking to the subway," said Bradford. "What makes a city competitive is the same thing that makes it livable. Quality of life is the whole game, and right now Toronto is losing it."

text:
TORONTO, ON | Standing on Kingston Road in Scarborough this morning, Brad Bradford committed to removing the red bus lanes on Kingston Road, Morningside Avenue, Kennedy Road and Midland Road, and returning 12 kilometres of Scarborough road to everyone who uses it.

The red lanes were never meant to be the plan. They were painted in the fall of 2020 as a stand-in for the Eglinton East LRT. The City's own report said so: the corridor was chosen because consultation for the LRT was already done, and a bus lane "would help build ridership for a future LRT alignment." The lanes were the bridge. The LRT was supposed to follow.

6 years later, there is no LRT. There is no provincial funding. There is no federal funding. There is no construction date. In April, the province said the line isn't on the province's priority list. NDP Mayor Chow's answer was a new name, a $10 million design budget and a working group. In the same stretch of months, the waterfront's LRT received $3 billion in committed funding. Scarborough received a rebrand, and the red paint stayed.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET SCARBOROUGH MOVING BY BUILDING REAL RAPID TRANSIT AND REMOVING RED BUS LANES: "SCARBOROUGH WAS PROMISED AN LRT. IT GOT RED PAINT."

text:
"Scarborough was promised an LRT. It got red paint," said Bradford. "The lanes were supposed to be temporary. They were supposed to build ridership for a train that was coming. The train never came, because this Mayor never fought for it. So the temporary fix became permanent, and the people stuck in traffic beside an empty red lane are paying for a promise City Hall broke."

Toronto drivers lost 100 hours to congestion last year, more than 4 full days, and it got worse than the year before. In Scarborough, where distances are long and transit options are thin, the time tax hits hardest. It's the parent who misses bedtime because of traffic on Morningside. It's the shift worker on Kingston Road who leaves an hour early and still clocks in late. It's the UTSC student who spends more time getting to campus than in class. Nobody voted for that. Nobody at City Hall can tell them where the time went.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET SCARBOROUGH MOVING BY BUILDING REAL RAPID TRANSIT AND REMOVING RED BUS LANES: "SCARBOROUGH WAS PROMISED AN LRT. IT GOT RED PAINT."

text:
As mayor, Bradford will direct City staff and the TTC to immediately remove the red bus lanes on Kennedy Road and Midland Road, which are now redundant. He will also remove the red bus lanes on the Kingston Road and Morningside Avenue, changing those lanes to High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) lanes. Brad’s plan will maintain the red lanes on Eglinton Avenue East because it has more buses than any other road in Scarborough.

He will keep this plan in place until the Eglinton East LRT is funded and under construction, and he has already committed to making Scarborough’s LRT Toronto's top transit priority. As mayor, Bradford will make a personal funding push to Queen's Park and Ottawa in his first 100 days with a commitment to get shovels in the ground by 2030. Scarborough gets its road back now and its train for real, instead of paint forever and a train never.

Scarborough residents pay more and get less. NDP Mayor Chow raised property taxes nearly 20 per cent, the largest in the city's history, and if she's re-elected she'll raise them another 20 per cent at least. For that, Scarborough got red paint on the road and a rename on a map.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET SCARBOROUGH MOVING BY BUILDING REAL RAPID TRANSIT AND REMOVING RED BUS LANES: "SCARBOROUGH WAS PROMISED AN LRT. IT GOT RED PAINT."

text:
"Olivia Chow stood on the debate stage and declared that Toronto has reached its full potential," said Bradford. "Tell that to someone sitting in traffic on Kingston Road at 5:30 on a Tuesday, looking at an empty red lane that was supposed to be a train by now. Toronto isn't broken. It's stuck. And nowhere is it more stuck than in Scarborough."

"We're on the cusp of change. Change is within our grasp," said Bradford. "To change the city, we need to change the mayor. On October 26th, Scarborough can choose a mayor who gets it moving. Not later. Right now."

“Toronto isn’t broken. It’s stuck,” said Bradford after the debate. “Residents give this city their time, their talent and their taxes, and every year they pay more and get less. I’m running because I believe Toronto’s best days are ahead of us. We’re on the cusp of change. Change is within our grasp. But to change the city, we need to change the mayor.”

The province has never given the City of Toronto more money than it has over the past 3 years. NDP Mayor Chow still raised property taxes nearly 20%, the largest increase in the city’s history. If she’s re-elected she’ll raise them another 20% at least. In the same 3 years, food bank visits climbed to 4.1 million, up 340% since 2019. The money came in, the taxes went up, and families are lining up for groceries. Where did the money go?
doc_title: BRADFORD: TORONTO’S BEST DAYS ARE AHEAD OF US, IF WE CHOOSE THEM

text:
Bradford’s plan starts with affordability. A property tax freeze in year 1, for homes and businesses. Water bills cut 25%, about $300 a year for the average household. The land transfer tax eliminated on homes below the $1.1 million average price, the biggest opportunity to buy a home this city has ever offered, by saving about $18,000. “Respecting your tax dollars doesn’t mean doing less for people. It means doing things properly,” continued Bradford. “Ontario modernized its budget 20 years ago. Ottawa did it 30 years ago. City Hall still runs on a system that lets $1.6 billion holes open up and nobody can tell you where the money went. I’m a city planner by training. I know how cities are supposed to work, and I know this one can work a lot better than it does. That’s not a cut. That’s a modern city government that earns the taxes it collects.”

text:
A more affordable city has to be a safer city. As Mayor, Bradford will take his seat on the Toronto Police Services Board, put 1,000 more front line officers on the street and a visible police presence at every subway station, and go after the repeat violent offenders who are terrorizing the same neighbourhoods over and over. And it has to be a city that moves: a 15 minute service guarantee on the TTC, and a single point of accountability for construction, with published timelines and consequences when they slip.

“A city that is not safe is not free,” said Bradford. “And a city where you spend 2 hours a day in traffic that nobody can explain is a city taxing your time on top of your money. Fix them, and Toronto takes off.”

text:

The Mayor held him responsible for things that happened before he was first elected in 2018, and for decisions made at Queen’s Park. text:
TORONTO, October 20, 2026 | If you ride the subway, you know the feeling. The train leaves the station, picks up speed, and then slows to a crawl for no reason you can see. It creeps along for a minute or 2, then speeds up again. That is a slow zone.

Brad Bradford today committed that a Bradford administration will set a standard of zero slow zones on Toronto's subway, publish the count every month, and pay for the track reconstruction the system has been waiting on through the modernized budget he announced on October 1. Bradford made the announcement near Davisville Station in Toronto–St. Paul’s as part of his “25/7” tour of the entire city during the final week of this campaign.

A slow zone, or what the TTC calls a reduced speed zone, is a stretch of track where inspectors have found a problem and trains are ordered to slow from their normal 40 to 65 km/h to as little as 15 km/h until the track is repaired and inspected again. Each one adds up to three minutes to a trip, by the TTC's own estimate. Some are gone in a few days. Others sit for weeks or months, because the equipment needed to fix them is out of service or because the repair was temporary and the problem came back.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET TORONTO'S SUBWAY BACK UP TO SPEED

text:
As of October 14, the TTC lists 13 of them on the subway. 11 are on Line 1, the Yonge-University line, which carries more than 650,000 riders a day and is the busiest rapid transit line in Canada. In five of them, trains are held to 15 km/h. Three have no repair date at all.

This is not new. It has been the story of the entire Chow administration. The TTC imposed 296 slow zones between January 2023 and September 2024, hit 34 at once in the summer of 2024, and has sat at about a dozen ever since. Three years and three budgets later, there has been no noticeable improvement. And riders have never been asked to give up more of their subway to get there: early weeknight closures and weekend shutdowns are now routine, people replan their nights out and their weekends around a subway that isn't open, and the slow zones keep coming.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET TORONTO'S SUBWAY BACK UP TO SPEED

text:
"Your time is the one thing City Hall can't give back to you," said Bradford. "Right now the subway crawls at 15 kilometres an hour between Eglinton and Davisville, between Bloor and Rosedale, between Royal York and Islington. Imagine if the speed limit on our roads was changed to 15 km/hr because we didn’t maintain them properly? Allowing this to happen is disrespectful to transit riders.”

“The TTC's official position is that there will never be zero slow zones. I don't accept that,” said Bradford. “Boston cleared more than 200 slow zones in 12 months because they set the target at zero. A target of a dozen gets you a dozen. I'm setting the target at zero and I'm going to publish the number every month so you can hold me to it."

City Hall and the TTC promised a subway that ran at full speed for the FIFA World Cup. For four weeks, it did. During the tournament the count fell to two, the lowest in three years. But within weeks, it was climbing again. By August 25, the count stood at 18. Transit analyst Steve Munro has documented that a regular quarterly track inspection was deferred so its results would not trigger new slow orders just before the games.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET TORONTO'S SUBWAY BACK UP TO SPEED

text:
"They pretended to fix the subway when the world showed up to Toronto, then let all the people who pay for it deal with the problems after," said Bradford. "That tells you everything about whose commute matters at City Hall. Olivia Chow stood on the debate stage and declared that Toronto has reached its full potential. On Line 1, that potential is 15 kilometres an hour."

The cause is well documented. The oldest outdoor sections of Line 1 and Line 2 still sit on wooden ties and ballast rather than a concrete base, so the track shifts with the weather and the same five stretches go back under slow orders every season. The work car fleet needed to repair them was pulled from service in April after hydraulic spills, even as spare subway cars sit in TTC yards. The same work car shortage is why the TTC's own report says the rollout of cellular service in the tunnels is at risk and has slipped into 2027. And $37.3 billion of the TTC's own 15-year capital plan, 69% of it, has no funding behind it, while more than $1 billion of the City's 2025 capital budget sat unspent.

A Bradford administration will:
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET TORONTO'S SUBWAY BACK UP TO SPEED

text:
-
Set a zero slow zone standard for the subway, adopted by the TTC board in the first 100 days, with every slow order carrying a published reason and a published repair date. No more "TBD."

-
Publish a monthly slow zone report showing the number of zones, how long each has been in force, and the total hours riders have lost to them, by line.

-
Order an independent track condition audit, public within the first 100 days, setting out what can be repaired and what has to be rebuilt, and the state of the work car fleet.

-
Launch a Subway Track Renewal Program to rebuild the chronic outdoor sections on a concrete base (direct fixation track) so the slow zones stop coming back, starting in the 2027 capital budget.

-
Renew the TTC's work car fleet by converting spare subway cars into work cars now, so the shortage ends in months rather than years, buying the TTC its own track inspection equipment so it stops renting and waiting in line behind other cities, and getting the delayed rollout of cellular service in the tunnels back on schedule.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET TORONTO'S SUBWAY BACK UP TO SPEED

text:
-
Publish an annual closure calendar a year ahead, so crews get the windows to make permanent repairs and riders can plan around them, with replacement buses given priority on the road.

-
Never defer a track inspection for an event again. Inspections run on schedule and the results are published, whatever is on the calendar.

The plan is paid for inside the fiscal framework Bradford announced on October 1: a real separation of the operating and capital budgets, with long-lived infrastructure like subway track financed over its useful life under the tightest debt rules in the country, rather than paid for in cash out of this year's property taxes while the work waits. The operating budget balances every year. No new taxes. No service cuts.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL GET TORONTO'S SUBWAY BACK UP TO SPEED

text:
"There are two ways to beat slow zones. You get disciplined about track repair, or you spend the capital to rebuild the worst stretches on a concrete base so they stop coming back. I'm going to do both," said Bradford. "Toronto pays cash up front for 50-year assets out of this year's taxes, which is why $37 billion of the TTC's repair plan has no money behind it and a billion dollars sat unspent last year. Every province does this differently. So does Toronto Hydro. Modernize the budget and the track gets rebuilt now, not never."

"The province has never sent the City more money, and NDP Mayor Chow still raised property taxes nearly 20%, the largest increase in the city's history. If she's re-elected she'll raise them another 20% at least. You are paying more and getting less, and you feel it every time the train slows to a crawl," said Bradford. "The Mayor has made her peace with less. I have not. Toronto isn't broken. It's stuck. We're on the cusp of change. Change is within our grasp. To change the city, we need to change the mayor."

TORONTO, ON | Brad Bradford today announced that as mayor he will eliminate Toronto's Municipal Land Transfer Tax on the value of a principal residence below the average Toronto home price, $1.1 million in 2025. If you're buying your first home, or you're a Toronto homeowner selling one home to buy another, you would pay no Municipal Land Transfer Tax on the first $1.1 million of the purchase. On a home at the threshold, that's about $18,000 back.

“Three of four Toronto renters don’t believe they’ll ever be able to afford to buy a home here. I refuse to accept that’s the best we can do. I’m running for mayor to make life more affordable and restore the dream of homeownership,” said Bradford.
doc_title: Brad Bradford will eliminate Toronto's land transfer tax for the average homebuyer

text:
Toronto is the only city in Canada that charges its own land transfer tax on top of the province's. It's collected on closing day, in cash, on top of the down payment, legal fees and the moving truck, on a purchase that's already stretched most families to the limit. And the one bit of relief the City offers has been left to rot. The first-time buyer rebate was set at $400,000 in 2008 and hasn't been touched since. Back then it covered most homes in the city. Today it fully exempts only 2.6% of them. Bradford's plan takes that from 2.6% of homes to as many as two thirds.

"When a family or a young worker finally scrapes together a down payment on a condo, the last thing they should hear at the lawyer's office is that City Hall wants another five figures before they get the keys," said Bradford. "Over the past six years, I’ve tried four times to give first-time buyers a tax break. And every chance she had, Olivia Chow voted it down. That's status quo thinking, and it's why a generation of Torontonians is getting priced out of the city they grew up in. We're going to fix it."
doc_title: Brad Bradford will eliminate Toronto's land transfer tax for the average homebuyer

text:
The plan has two parts. First, the first-time buyer rebate is expanded from a fixed $400,000 to the previous year's average Toronto sale price, and it moves with the market every year so it never falls out of date again. Most first-time buyers in Toronto are buying condos, well under the average price, which means for most of them the municipal land transfer tax disappears entirely.

Second, a new Principal Residence Rebate extends the same break to Toronto homeowners who sell their home to buy another one in the city. A senior who no longer needs the family home can downsize without a land transfer tax penalty if they buy again in Toronto, which frees that home up for a young family. A couple who bought a condo to get their foot in the door can move up to a house when the kids arrive. Today the tax punishes both moves and keeps people stuck in homes that no longer fit – or worse, push them to buy a home outside of Toronto. This is a tax cut for people who already live here and want to stay.
doc_title: Brad Bradford will eliminate Toronto's land transfer tax for the average homebuyer

text:
It's fair, and it's targeted. Investors and landlords who own more than one Toronto property, who make up 29% of purchases in this city, don't get the exemption. Neither do corporations or commercial buyers. Existing rates continue to apply on the value above $1.1 million, and the new higher rates NDP Mayor Chow introduced on homes over $3 million stay in place. Bradford’s tax break is for people who are going to live in the home.

The tax reduction would take effect for purchases from today, subject to Council approval. Bradford is setting the date now so that nobody who's ready to buy or sell puts their life on hold for a month waiting for the election.

"This is the tax cut Toronto can actually afford, because we're paying for it with money City Hall is already collecting," said Bradford.
doc_title: Brad Bradford will eliminate Toronto's land transfer tax for the average homebuyer

text:
Under NDP Mayor Chow, the answer to affordability has been to take more. text:
BACKGROUND: ELIMINATING THE LAND TRANSFER TAX ON HOMES BELOW THE AVERAGE PRICE

What it is: the Municipal Land Transfer Tax is eliminated on the value of an eligible principal residence below the average Toronto home price in the previous year, $1.1 million for 2025 sales. Existing rates continue to apply on value above that threshold. The rates introduced in December 2025 on homes above $3 million remain in place.

Who qualifies: first-time buyers, and existing Toronto homeowners who purchase a new principal residence in Toronto having sold their current one, or signed a firm and binding agreement of sale for it, within the previous six months (the Principal Residence Rebate). Buyers sign an affidavit, as first-time buyers do today. Co-ops and non-profits are eligible. Multi-property owners and landlords (29% of Toronto purchases), corporations and commercial transactions are not.

How many homes: more than two thirds of resale homes in Toronto sold below the 2025 average price of $1.1 million, according to TRREB data. The current first-time buyer rebate, fixed at $400,000 since 2008, fully exempts about 2.6% of homes.
doc_title: Brad Bradford will eliminate Toronto's land transfer tax for the average homebuyer

text:
What it's worth: on a home at the $1.1 million threshold, the saving is approximately $18,000.

Timing: applies to purchases with an agreement dated on or after September 29, 2026, subject to Council approval. For the Principal Residence Rebate, the sale of the existing home must also be agreed after that date, so that transactions already completed before the announcement do not receive a windfall.

Cost and funding: the exemption reduces Municipal Land Transfer Tax revenue by approximately $300 million a year. It is fully funded through Bradford’s plan outlined yesterday to modernize Toronto’s budget. This includes changes to amortize capital projects over their useful life instead of funding them from the current year’s operating budget and through dividends received from the city’s new 100% publicly-owned water utility announced yesterday.
doc_title: Brad Bradford will eliminate Toronto's land transfer tax for the average homebuyer

text:
Why the Land Transfer Tax: it penalizes moving, raises transaction costs, and locks households into homes that no longer fit. It is also volatile, rising in booms and collapsing in downturns, which makes it a poor way to fund permanent city services. The Principal Residence Rebate follows the same principle as the United Kingdom's reduced stamp duty on main residence purchases.

Brad Bradford’s Record on the Municipal Land Transfer Tax

As a councillor, Bradford has repeatedly worked to reduce costs for first-time homebuyers. This includes:

January 2020: Seconding a motion by Councillor Mark Grimes to review and increase the First-Time Home Buyers’ Rebate. (2020.MM14.6)

December 2021: Supporting an amendment by Councillor Stephen Holyday to review and increase the First-Time Home Buyers’ Rebate. (2023.CC2.1, motion 10b; passed 21-5)

September 2023: Moving an amendment to increase the First-Time Home Buyers’ Rebate to $750,000. (2023.EX7.1, motion 9b; defeated 10-13; Olivia Chow voted against)

December 2025: Moving an amendment to increase the First-Time Home Buyers’ Rebate to $800,000. (2025.EX28.1, motion 5b; defeated 4-19; Olivia Chow voted against)

With the Canada Investment Summit just around the corner, Bradford announces the Toronto Youth Employment Challenge, a City Hall-led drive to mobilize the city's private sector to put young Torontonians to work

TORONTO, ON | Toronto is home to a generation of young, talented and motivated people who are eager to learn, work, build careers and raise families right here in the city. But with youth unemployment in Toronto above 15 per cent by the City's own reporting, and the share of young Canadians holding a job having fallen last year to its lowest level since 1998, City Hall is failing them.

Visiting TAMOGO Canada, a North York-based not-for-profit that provides settlement services and employment support, mayoral candidate Brad Bradford announced the Toronto Youth Employment Challenge: a mayor-led initiative that will mobilize Toronto's private sector and its 1.4 million-strong workforce to get young Torontonians the paycheques they're looking for.
doc_title: BRADFORD ANNOUNCES TORONTO YOUTH EMPLOYMENT CHALLENGE

text:
Young people in this city face a record-high cost of living, smothering congestion, scarce housing and now the worst youth job market in a generation, a combination that is driving talent away just as Toronto should be competing for it.

"Toronto must compete with the best cities in the world for talent and jobs. Instead, we're driving young, ambitious talent out of the city. Not because they stopped loving Toronto, but because they stopped believing it's a place where they can find a good job and build a good life," said Bradford.

"The response from Mayor Chow has been the status quo: accepting defeat, and pouring more money into the approach that got us here. I won't accept that, and young people shouldn't either. This is why City Hall needs to change how it works, with real solutions that use every advantage this city has, and the urgency young Torontonians deserve."

Bradford's plan: the Toronto Youth Employment Challenge, in five pillars. As Mayor, Bradford will:

-
Declare a public goal of creating 15,000 permanent full-time jobs for youth on his first day in office, creating accountability and calling on the city's employers to participate.
doc_title: BRADFORD ANNOUNCES TORONTO YOUTH EMPLOYMENT CHALLENGE

text:
-
Personally recruit 10 to 15 top CEOs as founding Anchor Partners, who will drive job creation and tap into a wealth of young, ambitious and ready-to-work Torontonians.

-
Build a public pledge registry and portal that puts Toronto youth job postings in one place, with a quarterly leaderboard of jobs pledged and jobs created.

-
Require that at least 30 per cent of internships, apprenticeships and Anchor Partner positions go to equity-deserving youth, in communities where youth unemployment across Canada ran between 23 and 26 per cent last year.

-
Hold employers accountable by publishing outcomes against pledges, with three-year renewal terms and working with delivery and community partners.

The Challenge requires no new taxpayer-funded jobs program. Employers fund the positions; the City funds only the coordination behind them, at under $750,000 a year. Toronto doesn't need to reinvent the wheel. In New York City, the New York Jobs CEO Council has hired more than 65,000 New Yorkers since 2021. text:
Days before the Prime Minister’s Canada Investment Summit, Bradford commits to a police sub-station at Union Station and says the investment case for Toronto is the city itself

TORONTO, ON | Four days before the first ever Canada Investment Summit brings the world’s largest investors to Toronto, mayoral candidate Brad Bradford stood overlooking Union Station with a simple message. Billions of dollars in global investment are looking for cities where they can answer a single question: is this somewhere my employees would want to live? Right now, he said, City Hall has left Toronto unable to answer it.

“When a company CEO picks a city to invest in, he or she considers a lot of things. Tax rates are on the list. But the top of the list, every time, is one question: is this somewhere my employees would want to live,” said Bradford. “And right now, we can’t look those executives in the eye and give an unconditional yes. That has to change, and on October 26 it can.”
doc_title: BRADFORD AT TORONTO’S FRONT DOOR: THE WORLD ARRIVES IN FOUR DAYS, AND CITY HALL HASN’T CLEANED UP FOR IT

text: There’s no better place to see it than Union Station. More than a quarter of a million people pass through it every day, more than any other transportation hub in Canada, in a building the City of Toronto owns. It’s a National Historic Site, built in an era when Toronto wanted the world to know it was going somewhere: a block-long colonnade on Front Street, a Great Hall four storeys high, the names of cities across the country carved into its stone. The day it opened in 1927, the Prince of Wales crossed the Atlantic to cut the ribbon, with the British Prime Minister at his side and Prime Minister Mackenzie King there to receive them.
doc_title: BRADFORD AT TORONTO’S FRONT DOOR: THE WORLD ARRIVES IN FOUR DAYS, AND CITY HALL HASN’T CLEANED UP FOR IT

text:
And for the century since, it’s the room where Toronto begins. First jobs. First days in Canada. Students in September, soldiers coming home, kids on the way to their first Jays game. The Great Hall can still stop a first-time visitor in their tracks, Bradford said. The trouble is everything on the way to it: the grime, the doorways, the smell every commuter recognizes and nobody at City Hall will name. None of it, he said, is the fault of the crews who scrub that building every night. They’re working as hard as anyone in Toronto. It’s the standard the building’s owner has decided to live with.

“They opened Union Station in 1927 with a prince and two prime ministers. That’s how much this city’s front door mattered. It’s still where new lives begin. Your first job. Your first day in Canada. But now the welcome is disorder,” said Bradford. “That’s not on the crews who work miracles in that station every night. That’s the standard City Hall decided to accept. That’s what a stuck city looks like.”
doc_title: BRADFORD AT TORONTO’S FRONT DOOR: THE WORLD ARRIVES IN FOUR DAYS, AND CITY HALL HASN’T CLEANED UP FOR IT

text:
The Canada Investment Summit, September 14 and 15, will gather sovereign funds, institutional investors and chief executives behind a stated ambition of $1 trillion in investment over five years. Bradford wants the summit to succeed. But Toronto is competing for every dollar against Montreal, Calgary and Vancouver, and against New York, London and Singapore, and nobody hands the host city the prize. The Prime Minister and the province are doing their parts, he said, while the host city’s Mayor has spent three years leaving the basics undone.

“The Mayor’s going to be at that summit getting her picture taken and her face on TV. That’s not the job. The job was over the past three years when she served as Mayor,” said Bradford. “Toronto doesn’t need a photo op participant. It needs a mayor who rolls up their sleeves and gets the work done.”

Bradford’s plan for the station, and the city around it, is already public. Today he added to it: as mayor, he will establish a Toronto Police substation at Union Station, a permanent, visible police presence inside the busiest building in the country, working alongside the station’s security and the TTC.
doc_title: BRADFORD AT TORONTO’S FRONT DOOR: THE WORLD ARRIVES IN FOUR DAYS, AND CITY HALL HASN’T CLEANED UP FOR IT

text:
It joins the TTC Safety Plan he has already put on the table, which includes:

-
Sworn officers at every subway station.

-
Safety and cleanliness standards for every station, published so riders can see exactly how their station is doing.

-
Real platform edge doors, starting with the full height pilot the TTC’s own study recommended.

-
And a money back guarantee when the TTC leaves riders standing fifteen minutes past the promise.

The rest of the answer to the investor’s question is just as concrete: mental health outreach teams working with police, so a person in crisis gets help and a commuter gets to work safely; advocating for increased voluntary and mandatory treatment options for individuals suffering from the health crisis of severe drug addiction; public targets for maintenance of parks and public spaces; and one front door for permits, with the fee refunded when the city misses its own deadline.
doc_title: BRADFORD AT TORONTO’S FRONT DOOR: THE WORLD ARRIVES IN FOUR DAYS, AND CITY HALL HASN’T CLEANED UP FOR IT

text:
“A quarter of a million people a day deserve to walk through that station and feel what a visitor felt in 1927: this is a city that has its act together,” said Bradford. “Police in the building. Standards on the wall. A front door Toronto is proud of. None of that is complicated. It’s just the job.”

“Toronto isn’t broken. It’s stuck,” said Bradford. “On September 14, the world comes to look at Toronto. On October 26, Torontonians decide what the world sees next. That’s the change on the ballot.”

text:
Mandatory treatment helps the person, helps first responders, helps our communities. Mayor Chow is slowing down a compassionate response.

TORONTO, ON | Brad Bradford today called for mandatory addiction treatment now, saying Toronto can't spend two more years stepping around people dying in its parks, on its streets and on its transit while help sits behind a 72-day wait. Bradford's call comes a day after Ontario's Big City Mayors asked the province, for the second time in two years, to review the Mental Health Act and the Health Care Consent Act, more or less, the same review the caucus requested in October 2024.

"Toronto needs mandatory addiction treatment for the most severe cases, and we need it now. Not after another study, not after another review, not after two more years of letters," said Bradford. "I appreciate that twenty-nine leaders must agree on every word in a communique, and a stern call for review is commendable. But to be clear, we don’t need a review to determine if this is a problem. We need reform to stop it from being one. We need beds, we need change to the law, and we need the will to act."
doc_title: BRADFORD CALLS FOR MANDATORY ADDICTION TREATMENT NOW: 'WE DON'T NEED ANOTHER REVIEW'

text:
"I'm a father. I can't step around an unconscious human being on the sidewalk, holding my daughters' hands, and teach them that's normal," said Bradford. "Some people look at our streets and talk about zombies. I won't. Those are people, somebody's kid, somebody's parent, and they need our help. It's time to bring order and compassion back to this city. We can have both. We must have both."

Two years into the review era, the crisis has deepened. Toronto paramedics responded to 350 suspected non-fatal overdose calls in January 2026, up 46 per cent from a year earlier, and April 2026 was the worst month since 2021. Ontarians seeking intensive residential treatment still wait an average of 16 days for an assessment and 72 days for admission.
doc_title: BRADFORD CALLS FOR MANDATORY ADDICTION TREATMENT NOW: 'WE DON'T NEED ANOTHER REVIEW'

text:
"Other mayors have stopped waiting. Ken Sim, the mayor of Vancouver, is putting involuntary care beds to his residents this fall, and he told his own premier: 'We don't need another study. We don't need another plan. We need meaningful action now,'" said Bradford. "He's right. And I agree with Wab Kinew, the NDP Premier of Manitoba, when he said, 'People suffering from meth addiction do not have the right to determine how the rest of us are going to live in our society.' A mayor in Vancouver. A premier in Manitoba. This isn't left versus right. It's leadership versus looking away."

"And where has Toronto been? For two years, the Mayor's answer has been letters asking for funding. To this day, I haven’t heard Olivia Chow say the word: mandatory," said Bradford. "Toronto doesn't need a consensus position. It needs a plan."

Bradford's plan, announced Friday, commits that as Mayor he will:

• Call on the province to introduce a mandatory treatment law covering adults whose severe addiction has stripped their capacity to make treatment decisions and who face a serious, near-term risk of harm, with the same independent review Ontario already provides for severe mental illness.
doc_title: BRADFORD CALLS FOR MANDATORY ADDICTION TREATMENT NOW: 'WE DON'T NEED ANOTHER REVIEW'

text:
• Fight for Toronto's full share of new residential treatment, withdrawal management and supportive housing beds, so treatment is there when people ask for it.

• Commit to at least 100 recovery house beds in Toronto: structured, live-in recovery homes where people can stay for up to a year, modelled on the recovery communities already operating in Alberta, fast-tracked through a new zoning class for accredited treatment and recovery homes and supported by funding from the provincial government and not-for-profit partners.

• Meet the crisis where it shows up by expanding co-response teams that pair police officers with mental health and addiction clinicians and embedding outreach workers on the TTC and in community with direct referral pathways into treatment.

• Hold Queen's Park to results: a commitment to continuous addiction medication through treatment and release, and independent, published evaluation written into the law from day one.
doc_title: BRADFORD CALLS FOR MANDATORY ADDICTION TREATMENT NOW: 'WE DON'T NEED ANOTHER REVIEW'

text:
On the mayors' call for an emergency declaration, Bradford said he will support anything that gets beds built faster: "But you can't declare your way out of a seventy-two day wait. Declarations don't treat anyone. Access to critical care does."

"When addiction gets so severe that someone no longer has the capacity to make important life decisions on their own, and they are at risk of losing their life, the rest of us have a collective responsibility to help by making compassionate life-saving decisions for them, and getting them the help they need," said Bradford. "That's how we help people get better, and that's how we give parks back to families and make our city feel safe again."

Learn more at bradford26.ca.

text:
New 50 per cent tariffs threaten Toronto industries

TORONTO – July 22, 2026 – Mayoral candidate Brad Bradford supports urgent action by Ottawa, Queen's Park and City Hall to quickly protect Toronto workers and manufacturers from the latest round of U.S. tariffs.

On July 20, U.S. President Donald Trump announced additional 50 per cent tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, effective August 19. The tariffs will apply even to goods that meet CUSMA rules of origin. Targeted products include clothing, furniture, cement, dairy, wine and hockey equipment, putting Toronto manufacturing jobs and local suppliers directly at risk.

The damage has already started. Toronto apparel makers that design and manufacture their products here have paused shipments to American customers. Furniture manufacturers and building-material suppliers that serve customers on both sides of the border are now assessing their exposure.
doc_title: BRADFORD CALLS FOR URGENT ACTION TO PROTECT TORONTO JOBS FROM NEW U.S. TARIFFS

text:
"Donald Trump is picking another fight with Canada, and Toronto workers shouldn't be left to pay the bill," said Bradford. "The people who cut, sew, build and ship Canadian products need action from every level of government. Ottawa and Queen's Park must help businesses losing orders. TORONTO, ON, October 18, 2026. This morning in downtown Toronto, mayoral candidate Brad Bradford announced that he would implement common-sense measures to get Toronto moving, including starting subway service two hours earlier at 6 a.m. on the day of the marathon.

More than 31,000 runners from over 75 countries came to Toronto this weekend for the TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon, joined by thousands of volunteers, families and supporters, all headed for the downtown core early on a Sunday morning. The City of Toronto told them to leave the car at home and take transit. The problem is: the subways didn’t open until 8 am, so attendees were stuck without a serious transit option.

The TTC's own service notice for the weekend states that "subway service does not start until 8 a.m." Guess what else starts at 8 a.m.? The marathon. Meanwhile, the City closed Lake Shore Boulevard from 5 a.m., closed Bathurst, Bloor and Yonge from 7 a.m., and diverted more than 2 dozen bus and streetcar routes from 4 a.m. It could figure out how to do all of that, but it could not open the subway two hours earlier.

"Everyone at City Hall knew the date of the marathon for a year. Everyone knew 31,000 people were coming. Opening the subway at 6 a.m. on marathon morning is common sense, and the Mayor or her staff didn’t think it was important," said Toronto mayoral candidate Brad Bradford. “When I’m mayor, we’ll start subway service at 6 a.m. on the day of the marathon to give people better options.”

text:
Plan would replace Toronto's pre-dawn dash for summer camp with a fair, modern, family-first system

TORONTO: Every spring, tens of thousands of Torontonians set an alarm for 6:30 a.m., log onto a highly sought-after registration portal, and press refresh. If they’re smart, they have a laptop, iPad and cell phone all going at the same time – tripling their chances. If it’s a two adult household, both are doing it at the same time on separate devices. Are they trying to secure a ticket to the world cup game or a Taylor Swift concert? No. They’re trying to crack the Toronto Recreation Summer Camp sign-up. The “Hunger Games” of City Hall registration.

Signing your children up for a City of Toronto-run summer camp has become an Olympic skill, with families sharing tricks on WhatsApp groups and over text messages. Within minutes, the most sought-after spots are always gone. Hours later, parents are still in hidden queues, watching the screen, hoping the session at their local community centre has not vanished.
doc_title: BRADFORD: END THE REGISTRATION SPRINT

text:
It would be comical, if it didn’t eat up hours away from what matters most, and didn’t leave families high and dry come the summer months. This is the time tax. Hours stolen from families before they have even started their day. Time they will never get back, levied by a system the Mayor’s Office refuses to fix.

Today Mayoral candidate Brad Bradford announced a plan to end the Registration Sprint and replace it with a system built for the families it is supposed to serve.

“The City of Toronto has built a registration system that punishes the parents who need it most. A single mother working a morning shift cannot sit at a screen at 7 a.m. A new family in Scarborough does not know which catchment they are in, or that they had to pre-register. The Mayor has made her peace with families racing the clock at sunrise. I have not.”

-Brad Bradford
doc_title: BRADFORD: END THE REGISTRATION SPRINT

text:
Fixing this isn’t like cracking the DaVinci code. There are jurisdictions that have figured it out: Washington, D.C. has a two-week registration window for summer camps in which every family has the same chance regardless of when they apply in that window. New York City uses the same model. Philadelphia rolled out a lottery at its highest-demand sites earlier this year. Bermuda announced its lottery in March. The technology exists. The model is proven. Toronto can do this.

Bradford's plan to end the Registration Sprint has three priorities.

1. A FAIR START. A multi-day registration window, followed by a transparent draw. No advantage to anyone with faster internet, an earlier alarm, or fewer obligations between 6:30 and 7:30 a.m. Sibling registrations can be linked, so brothers and sisters are placed together. Independent oversight of the draw, with results published.
doc_title: BRADFORD: END THE REGISTRATION SPRINT

text:
2. LOCAL ACCESS. Expand staggered registration by district and program category, so the parent in Etobicoke is not bidding against the parent in East York for the same gym at the same minute. Grow the Early Local Registration Initiative to all 37 free community recreation centres, providing priority access for the families who live closest.

3. A SYSTEM THAT WORKS FOR FAMILIES. Reorder your wishlist after you have built it. See your real position on the waitlist. Prove your Toronto residency once and carry it forward. See your Welcome Policy subsidy at checkout, automatically applied. A staffed help line during peak windows.

Recreation registration is, at its core, a cost of living issue. When parents aren’t able to access city-run programming, the alternative is a private day camp at three or four times the price. Families pay the time tax in lost hours, and pay it again in dollars when the system fails to deliver.

“I am the father of two young girls. My wife and I know how broken the system is, first-hand. But this is not about my family. It is about every family in this city.
doc_title: BRADFORD: END THE REGISTRATION SPRINT

text:
Other cities have already figured this out. Toronto can too. If I am fortunate enough to lead this city, you will have a mayor who fixes the small systems that make everyday life work. Because families are the bedrock of this city, and they deserve a city that is built for them.” -Brad Bradford

-
Cut red tape that slows down getting food programs into schools and community hubs that need them most;

-
Partner with community agencies and local growers to increase economic and community development benefits from the program; and

-
Report publicly on the program’s rollout and impact in Toronto, so families can see the funding translating into food in the hands of our kids.

The rising cost of living has forced too many Toronto families into difficult choices just to make ends meet.

"Every level of government has a role to play in making life affordable in our city. But under Mayor Chow, costs have gone up and taxes have risen nearly 20% in 3 years," Bradford said. "Toronto is stuck paying more and getting less. There’s more the City can do to lower costs for families, and that starts with change at City Hall."

Bradford also announced a commitment to address restrictive covenants in the grocery sector: private legal clauses, often attached to a property’s title when a grocery chain sells or leases a site, that bar any future occupant from operating a grocery store or supermarket.
doc_title: Bradford Pledges to Make Food More Affordable and Accessible for Toronto Families

text:
Research from the Competition Bureau and the Public Interest Advocacy Centre has identified dozens of these covenants across Canadian cities, including in Ontario, creating "food deserts" where neighbourhoods lose walkable access to affordable groceries simply because a competitor is legally barred from moving in.

"This isn’t about zoning or red tape. It’s a private contract sitting quietly on a piece of land, keeping a grocery store out and prices high for the people who live nearby," said Bradford. "If we’re serious about making food more affordable and accessible in this city, we have to deal with the barriers nobody’s talking about, not just the obvious ones."

Bradford said that, as mayor, he would:

-
Formally press the province to adopt Manitoba-style legislation voiding anti-competitive restrictive covenants and exclusivity clauses in the grocery sector, working in coalition with other Ontario municipalities facing food deserts;

-
Ensure the City never attaches restrictions limiting grocery use on any City-owned land it sells or leases for commercial development; and
doc_title: Bradford Pledges to Make Food More Affordable and Accessible for Toronto Families

text:
-
Use the City's economic development and planning tools to actively court independent and discount grocers into covenant-free sites in underserved neighbourhoods.

Building more homes in Toronto by getting bureaucracy out of the way

text:
As new tariffs hit the things Toronto makes, Bradford puts his own campaign to work for local businesses, and lays out the change at City Hall that would match the effort

TORONTO, ON | Five days after 50 per cent U.S. tariffs took effect on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods, mayoral candidate Brad Bradford stood on the workshop floor of Brave Leather, a Toronto maker of belts and leather goods, and called on Torontonians to stand together behind the city’s workers, shopkeepers, farmers and manufacturers, committing his own campaign to lead by example.

The new tariffs reach products previously protected under CUSMA and land directly on what Toronto makes: clothing, furniture, cement, dairy, wine and sporting goods.

The week since has only escalated: Washington has threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian cars and trucks to 50 per cent, and on Tuesday the federal government announced matching counter-tariffs on $27.6 billion of U.S. goods effective September 8, alongside $7.5 billion in new support for affected workers and businesses.
doc_title: BRADFORD RALLIES TORONTO BEHIND ITS MAKERS: “LET’S ALL DO OUR PART. I’LL START WITH MINE.”

text:
“This isn’t about pointing fingers. It’s about bringing this city together,” said Bradford. “Every consumer has a choice, and it takes a bit of work from each of us. Check the label. Pick the Ontario produce. Choose the shop around the corner instead of the click online from somewhere else. The people who invested in Toronto, who built their businesses here and hire here, need to see the love right now. Give it to them.”

Bradford said he isn’t waiting for election day to do his own part. His campaign has committed to:

-
Spotlight Toronto makers, shops and manufacturers regularly as this tariff war continues, using the platform of this race to put local businesses in front of the whole city. Today’s visit to Brave Leather, whose products sit squarely in the newly tariffed categories, is the first stop.

-
Buy Toronto and buy Canadian for everything the campaign itself purchases, wherever it’s available, from signs to sandwiches.

-
Invite Torontonians to send in the local businesses they love at info@bradford26.ca, so the campaign can share them and keep the spotlight moving.
doc_title: BRADFORD RALLIES TORONTO BEHIND ITS MAKERS: “LET’S ALL DO OUR PART. I’LL START WITH MINE.”

text:
-
Sit down with affected manufacturers, workers and business owners across the city in the coming weeks, so the response to this shock is built with the people living it.

“I’ve got a platform in this race, and the most useful thing I can do with it right now is use it to help the people who make things in this city,” said Bradford. “Canadians helping each other has always been bigger than politicians. But leadership means going first.”

Bradford also laid out the first steps on how he would match that effort at City Hall. As Mayor, he will:

-
Stand up a permanent City of Toronto tariff-response table with manufacturers, workers and industry representatives, in the room the day a shock hits, not weeks later. The table will also serve as one front door connecting Toronto businesses to the new federal and provincial tariff supports, so no employer is left to navigate them alone.
doc_title: BRADFORD RALLIES TORONTO BEHIND ITS MAKERS: “LET’S ALL DO OUR PART. I’LL START WITH MINE.”

text:
-
Deliver real property tax relief, not deferral, for every year the trade war is ongoing: 25 per cent relief for roughly 3,500 industrial businesses, helping employers weather the storm and keep people on payroll. Bradford first proposed this in a motion at City Council in February 2025, but it was voted down by Mayor Chow and her allies.

-
Get approvals done in weeks, not years, for manufacturers expanding or modernizing Toronto facilities.

-
Put the City’s full purchasing power behind Toronto- and Ontario-made goods: implement the Buy Ontario Act’s new municipal procurement requirements ahead of schedule, go further wherever trade rules permit, and publish where the City’s procurement dollars actually go. If we’re asking every family to check the label, City Hall should show its receipts too.

-
Partner with the Province to put Buy Ontario manufacturing supports to work for Toronto companies.

-
Give residents an honest accounting of the city’s reserves and a plan to rebuild them.
doc_title: BRADFORD RALLIES TORONTO BEHIND ITS MAKERS: “LET’S ALL DO OUR PART. I’LL START WITH MINE.”

text:
Bradford acknowledged the honest starting point for that work. The city enters this trade shock with its reserve funds drawn down by $1.7 billion to balance an election-year budget, the largest such drawdown in Toronto’s history, with the 2027 budget already opening roughly $1.1 billion short, and with the centrepiece of City Hall’s 2025 tariff response, an industrial property tax deferral, expired since last November, nine months before this round arrived.

Bradford’s case is that the city’s problem is not its people but its pace: Toronto enters this storm stuck, with permits measured in years, reserves spent before the rain came, and a tariff program that lapsed before the tariffs arrived. Change, he argues, is how the city gets unstuck.

“We can’t change what Washington does. But we can change how ready this city is for it. Change how City Hall spends, change how fast it moves, change who it shows up for. That’s what October 26th is: the day Torontonians get to make the change themselves,” said Bradford.

“Toronto isn’t broken. It’s stuck,” added Bradford. “On October 26th we can get it unstuck, and build a city we can all be proud of.”
doc_title: BRADFORD RALLIES TORONTO BEHIND ITS MAKERS: “LET’S ALL DO OUR PART. I’LL START WITH MINE.”

Bradford sets out a three-part plan for the half of Toronto that rents: enforce the renoviction rules the City already has, deliver a maximum heat standard with a cool room in every rental home, and give non-profit builders clear rules and early money to build. These build on his commitments to lower water bills for all residents, including renters, and save first-time homebuyers $18,000.

TORONTO, ON | Brad Bradford today set out a plan for the nearly 560,000 households that rent in Toronto, almost half the city. Four in 10 of them already spend more than 30% of their income keeping a roof over their heads. Bradford’s plan will make life more affordable for renters while protecting them from renovictions and extreme heat.

Under NDP Mayor Olivia Chow, property taxes went up nearly 20%, starting with 9.5%, the largest increase in the city’s history, pushing rent prices higher. Renters got the bill. They did not get the results.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES HIS PLAN FOR RENTERS: KEEP YOUR HOME. COOL YOUR HOME. BUILD MORE HOMES.

text: The City passed a renoviction licensing by-law in July 2025 and still cannot tell you how many renovictions it has stopped, because nobody publishes the results. 271,000 rental units sit in buildings with no air conditioning. Last summer the City’s air conditioner program delivered 489 units against 1,414 applications, turning away two-thirds of people who asked for help. Council has directed a maximum heat by-law for June 2027, and the Mayor’s own staff report says 90% of the landlords the City consulted intend to pass the cost on to tenants. She has no answer for that. And too many non-profit and co-op housing developers are stuck without the support required to get building new affordable homes, as Mayor Chow continues to focus on her bureaucratic public builder model.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES HIS PLAN FOR RENTERS: KEEP YOUR HOME. COOL YOUR HOME. BUILD MORE HOMES.

text:
“Half this city rents their home. NDP Mayor Chow decided that holding a press conference and passing a by-law was good enough, without doing the follow-up to make sure it worked. That is how Toronto got stuck,” said Brad Bradford, candidate for Mayor of Toronto. “Renters don’t need another announcement. They need someone to enforce the rules already on the books, make sure nobody is boiling in their own apartment in July, and get more homes built by people who aren’t going to flip the building in five years. My plan is focused around these pillars: Keep your home. Cool your home. Build more homes.”

Bradford’s plan for renters

Keep your home

-
Enforce the renoviction by-law the City already has. Bradford will increase transparency with a public dashboard, updated every quarter from Toronto Building: applications, licences issued and refused, investigations, charges, convictions, fines actually collected, and tenant compensation owed and paid. Published by address, with tenant privacy protected.

-
A costed staffing plan for Toronto Building so that when a tenant complains, somebody shows up. A rule nobody enforces is not protection.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES HIS PLAN FOR RENTERS: KEEP YOUR HOME. COOL YOUR HOME. BUILD MORE HOMES.

text:
-
Expand the eviction prevention programs that work and ensure they are appropriately funded. In 2025, Eviction Prevention in the Community (EPIC) kept 1,105 households in their homes and the Toronto Rent Bank approved 2,961 grants.

-
Ask Queen’s Park to toughen the evidence rules and penalties for bad-faith renovations and own-use evictions, and to resource the Landlord and Tenant Board so tenants get decisions in weeks, not months.

Cool your home

-
A maximum heat standard renters can count on: at least one cooled living space in every rental home. Modelled on New Westminster, B.C., where that room may not average more than 26 degrees overnight from April through October, and adapted for Toronto through public-health and legal review.

-
Delivered for Council approval by June 2027, the deadline Council already set, with a funded, phased implementation plan attached. Not another study. The phased plan will prioritize the oldest towers and Toronto Community Housing first.

-
Ask the Province to prohibit above-guideline rent increases for mandated cooling, and attach no-pass-through conditions to any cooling work the City helps pay for.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES HIS PLAN FOR RENTERS: KEEP YOUR HOME. COOL YOUR HOME. BUILD MORE HOMES.

text:
-
Expand the Air Conditioner Benefit for low-income seniors and people with medical need, and publish applications, approvals and units delivered every year so the program is measured by who got help, not who applied.

Build more homes

-
A predictable Non-Profit Density Framework so mission-driven builders get clear eligibility, standard terms and a financially tested approach to density, instead of a one-off negotiation for every site.

-
Expand the City’s revolving pre-development fund, which today offers about $10 million in interest-free loans of up to $50,000 per affordable home, with transparent terms and annual reporting. The money gets repaid and lent again. Non-profits have a pipeline of thousands of homes waiting on exactly this.

-
Publicly report the City’s housing progress more regularly and transparently, and change the main metric of success to keys in doors, not approvals on paper.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES HIS PLAN FOR RENTERS: KEEP YOUR HOME. COOL YOUR HOME. BUILD MORE HOMES.

text:
“Non-profit and co-op builders are the people who will still own the building in 40 years. They are not trying to flip it. And City Hall makes them beg, site by site, for density it should be offering as a matter of policy,” said Bradford. “Give them the rules, give them the early money, and count every home. That is how you build housing people can afford and keep.”

Today’s commitments build on two pieces of Bradford’s fiscal plan that already put money in renters’ pockets.

-
The water bill cut reaches renters. Bradford’s 25% water bill cut, about $300 a year for the average household, is applied to every resident’s bills, including Toronto Community Housing and Toronto Seniors Housing. For tenants whose landlord pays the water bill, Bradford has already written to Minister Flack asking the Province to extend section 131 of the Residential Tenancies Act, which forces a rent reduction when a landlord’s property taxes go down, to permanent municipal water rate cuts. Landlord’s water bill goes down, the rent goes down. No cost to the Province, no cost to landlords.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES HIS PLAN FOR RENTERS: KEEP YOUR HOME. COOL YOUR HOME. BUILD MORE HOMES.

text:
-
The biggest opportunity ever to buy a first home in Toronto. The City’s first-time buyer rebate was written in 2008 and today fully covers only 2.6% of homes. Bradford will eliminate the Municipal Land Transfer Tax on the value of an average home, saving people $18,000. It is the largest expansion of the first-time buyer break in the city’s history, and it is aimed at the renter trying to get over the line.

The province has never sent the City more money. NDP Mayor Chow still raised property taxes nearly 20%, starting with 9.5%, the largest increase in the city’s history. If she’s re-elected she’ll raise them another 20% at least. Food bank visits are up 340% since 2019, 4.1 million last year alone. And last month, Olivia Chow stood on the debate stage and declared that Toronto has reached its full potential.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES HIS PLAN FOR RENTERS: KEEP YOUR HOME. COOL YOUR HOME. BUILD MORE HOMES.

text:
“Tell that to the renter who got an N13 in the mail, or the senior who spent August in a 32-degree apartment waiting on an air conditioner that never came,” said Bradford. “The Mayor passed by-laws and called it progress. I’m going to deliver them with more transparency and accountability than we’ve seen in years. And I’m going to make sure a renter in this city gets the water bill cut, gets a real shot at a first home, and gets a City Hall that keeps its word. Toronto isn’t broken. It’s stuck. We’re on the cusp of change. Change is within our grasp. To change the city, we need to change the mayor.”

Learn more at bradford26.ca.
