text:
TORONTO, ON | This morning in Don Valley West, Brad Bradford sat down with a group of mothers to talk about the things they think about every day. Whether their kids are safe walking to school, riding the subway or on the playground. Whether they'll make it home in time for dinner. Whether their kids will find a first job and a first home in the city they grew up in. Then he released his plan for the first 100 days of a Bradford administration: five priorities, each with concrete steps, a mechanism and a timeline.

“The moms I sat down with today aren't asking for miracles. They're asking for a city that works,” said Bradford. “Job #1 is public safety. Because the data tells us we're not safe enough, and a city that is not safe is not free. Then we get Toronto moving, we find out where the money went, we fix how the budget is built and we put this city's young people to work. Change starts on day one.”

THE FIRST 100 DAYS

1.

Public safety.

Auto theft is up.

Assaults are up.

Break and enters are up.

Home invasions are on the rise.

Half a million more people have moved to Toronto and there are no more police officers on the street.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES PLAN FOR FIRST 100 DAYS: 5 PRIORITIES, STARTING WITH PUBLIC SAFETY

text:
People don't feel safe, and the numbers say they're right.

In week one, Bradford will call in the TTC and the Chief of Police and work with them to deliver a transit safety strategy that puts a police officer at every subway station.

He will take the seat on the police board that’s reserved for the mayor by law.

He will work with the province and Toronto Police Service to begin the recruitment that gets Toronto to 1,000 net new front line officers by the end of a first term, with the first recruits in the pipeline before the 100 days are out, and open talks with the province on a Toronto campus of the Ontario Police College so the city can train its own officers again.

He will personally carry Toronto's demand for bail reform to the Premier and the Prime Minister.

And he will formally ask the province for more voluntary treatment options and a mandatory addiction treatment law for the most severe cases, with real safeguards, while beginning work on at least 100 recovery house beds in Toronto.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES PLAN FOR FIRST 100 DAYS: 5 PRIORITIES, STARTING WITH PUBLIC SAFETY

text: 2. The Scarborough LRT and transit that works. Bradford will personally carry the business case for the Scarborough Eglinton East LRT to the Premier and the Prime Minister in his first 100 days. The plan exists. The route is drawn. The environmental assessment is done. What's been missing is a mayor who fights for it. He will begin removing the red bus lanes on Kingston Road, Morningside Avenue, Kennedy Road and Midland Road that were handed to Scarborough in place of the LRT it was promised. He will direct the TTC to deliver a plan to get rid of subway slow zones and put the 15-minute service guarantee in place. And he will name a single point of accountability for construction across the city, with published timelines and real consequences for projects that drag on for years. The time tax is the mom who misses bedtime because the streetcar sat in traffic. Nobody voted for it, and nobody gets those hours back.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES PLAN FOR FIRST 100 DAYS: 5 PRIORITIES, STARTING WITH PUBLIC SAFETY

text: 3. A line by line review of City Hall spending. On day one, Bradford will order the first full, independent, line by line review of City Hall spending since 2011, with the results made public. The province has never given the City of Toronto more money than it has over the past 3 years. NDP Mayor Chow still raised property taxes nearly 20%, the largest increase in the city's history. If she's re-elected she'll raise them another 20% at least. Food bank visits are up 340% since 2019, 4.1 million last year alone. Where did the money go? $11 million on software licences for people who no longer work for the city. $5 million on recycling bin stickers. Nobody is minding the books. A Bradford administration will treat every dollar families send to City Hall with the respect it deserves.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES PLAN FOR FIRST 100 DAYS: 5 PRIORITIES, STARTING WITH PUBLIC SAFETY

text: 4. A modern budget. Bradford's first budget, tabled within the first 100 days, will begin modernizing the City's budget with a true separation of operating and capital spending, the way Ontario did years ago and Prime Minister Mark Carney does. NDP Mayor Chow came into office with a $1.8 billion hole in the budget and is leaving with a $1.6 billion hole, with no plan to close it. His administration’s first budget will freeze property taxes for homes and businesses, start reducing water bills by up to 25%, about $300 a year for the average household, and bring the elimination of the land transfer tax on homes below $1.1 million to Council, about $18,000 back on closing day for a family buying their first home. Families don't sit at the kitchen table talking about capital budgets. But they expect the person running a government larger than four provinces to understand how one works.
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES PLAN FOR FIRST 100 DAYS: 5 PRIORITIES, STARTING WITH PUBLIC SAFETY

text:
5. More private-sector jobs for youth. Youth unemployment in Toronto is at 17%, four points higher than the national average. On his first day in office, Bradford will launch the Toronto Youth Employment Challenge and set a public goal of 5,000 new private-sector youth jobs in year 1 and 15,000 by the end of the term, with 30% of placements reserved for young people facing the steepest barriers. He will personally recruit 10 to 15 CEOs as founding Anchor Partners. Over the past week, Bradford has already recruited the CEOs of two leading Toronto employers, Atlantic Packaging and Borrowell, to serve as anchor partners.

“I'm a city planner by training. I know how cities are supposed to work, and I know what it takes to get City Hall moving,” said Bradford. “None of this requires a year of study. It requires a decision. Residents will see a credible plan for crime, a credible plan for congestion and a credible plan for cost in the first 100 days. Not platitudes. Numbers, dates and the names of the people responsible.”
doc_title: BRADFORD RELEASES PLAN FOR FIRST 100 DAYS: 5 PRIORITIES, STARTING WITH PUBLIC SAFETY

text:
Olivia Chow stood on the debate stage and declared that Toronto has reached its full potential. Bradford rejects that. A city where parents drive kids who used to take the bus to school is not our full potential. The worst commutes in North America is not our full potential. A generation of young people doing the math on whether to stay is not our full potential.

“Toronto isn't broken. It's stuck. And for three years, the people running this city have made their peace with that. I have not,” said Bradford. “We're on the cusp of change. Change is within our grasp. But to change the city, we need to change the mayor. In 4 days, Toronto gets to choose. And on day one, we get to work.”

Learn more at bradford26.ca.

text:
Campaign website goes live at bradford26.ca

TORONTO – Toronto City Councillor and candidate for Mayor, Brad Bradford today launched his campaign’s website at bradford26.ca and set out the foundational vision of his campaign: a Toronto residents can be proud of again.

The website launch follows Bradford’s nomination filing on Friday, May 1, the first day of the nomination period. Bradford was one of the first in the door at the City Clerk’s Office. Mayor Olivia Chow has not filed her own nomination papers, and despite repeated questions from reporters, has declined to confirm whether she will seek re‑election.
doc_title: BRADFORD UNVEILS CAMPAIGN VISION FOR “A TORONTO WE CAN BE PROUD OF AGAIN”

text:
“I filed on Friday because Toronto deserves a campaign in the open, on the public record, and frankly not on the public dime. The Mayor of this city has not done that. She has been asked, more than once, whether she is running. She will not say. You cannot use the Mayor’s Office, the Mayor’s Budget, the Mayor’s calendar, and the Mayor’s staff to do the work of a campaign and then refuse to admit it is a campaign. Toronto needs better than that and once again, the Mayor is asking Torontonians to accept less than what they deserve. On October 26, Torontonians will have a choice: keep what you have got or demand better.” – Brad Bradford

Bradford also called on the City and on Mayor Chow to address the emergence of third parties attacking his candidacy on Facebook and in the news, including by groups that have not registered as a third party under the City’s election rules.

“There is a third party in this race posting attacks against me without registering as a third party. The City has rules. The Mayor is silent. If the people posting these attacks want to be in this race, they can register and play by the rules like everyone else. That is the standard.” – Brad Bradford
doc_title: BRADFORD UNVEILS CAMPAIGN VISION FOR “A TORONTO WE CAN BE PROUD OF AGAIN”

text:
Bradford framed today’s launch as an answer to two questions Torontonians keep asking: what kind of city are we becoming, and who is going to do the work to fix it. He said pride in Toronto cannot be declared from City Hall. It has to be earned, block by block, service by service, day by day.

The campaign continues to be anchored by three priorities. The Three C’s: Crime, Congestion, and Cost. Bradford said these are not abstractions or talking points. They are the issues every Torontonian feels every day, and they are the ones a Mayor is elected to deliver on.

Crime, because the confidence Torontonians once felt walking home, riding the subway, or watching their kids in the park has been quietly eroded, and the city cannot afford to keep pretending it has not. Congestion, because the time tax City Hall levies on residents, in road closures no one coordinates and transit that does not run on time, climbs higher every year. Cost, because families and small businesses are being asked to pay more for a city that delivers less.
doc_title: BRADFORD UNVEILS CAMPAIGN VISION FOR “A TORONTO WE CAN BE PROUD OF AGAIN”

text:
Toronto is in a competition we cannot afford to lose. For talent. For investment. For the families deciding where to put down roots and the businesses deciding where to grow. text:
A plan to restore the country’s busiest public square, honour the Canadians who built this country, and ask the property taxpayer for nothing.

TORONTO, ON. Mayoral candidate Brad Bradford today released a plan to restore the public square at Yonge and Dundas, currently named Sankofa Square, as a clean, safe and vibrant heart of the city, and to rename it Toronto Square. The plan would be delivered through a partnership with an iconic Canadian brand, at no cost to the property taxpayer.

The square sits on the busiest intersection in the country, where more than 100,000 people cross every day. Under the plan, the City would set published cleaning and safety standards for the space, look to establish a permanent police substation staffed by officers already on the force, expand outreach and mental health support for people in crisis, and fill the square with a year-round calendar of commerce, culture, food, retail and live performance.
doc_title: BRADFORD UNVEILS PLAN TO CLEAN UP, MAKE SAFE AND RENAME YONGE AND DUNDAS AS TORONTO SQUARE

text:
“This is the first thing visitors see of our city, and right now it tells them we have given up,” said Bradford. “It is dirty, it is unsafe, and families walk a little faster to get through it. That is not a tragedy. It is a choice, and I am making a different one.”

Between events and advertising, the square’s screens would carry a rotating tribute to the Canadians who built this country and shaped the world, among them Viola Desmond, Terry Fox, Tom Longboat, Sir Frederick Banting, and Lucie and Thornton Blackburn.

“A great public square should remind us who we are,” said Bradford. “Canadians from every community that has made this city home, honoured by name, in lights, in the heart of downtown, every single day.”

Honourees would be chosen by an independent, broadly representative panel rather than by the Mayor’s office. The renaming would require a vote of City Council, which Bradford committed to bringing forward and championing.
doc_title: BRADFORD UNVEILS PLAN TO CLEAN UP, MAKE SAFE AND RENAME YONGE AND DUNDAS AS TORONTO SQUARE

text:
The plan carries no cost to the property taxpayer. The cleanup, the programming and the renaming would be financed through a partnership with an iconic Canadian brand, supported by the advertisers and businesses that profit from the corner. It mirrors the approach the City itself adopted at the last renaming, when any cost above its own budget was to be carried by private partners and in-kind support. The officers who staff the new substation would be drawn from existing Toronto Police Service resources and directed to the busiest public space in the city.

“Not one dollar of this lands on your property tax bill,” said Bradford. “The people who profit from that corner can help us restore it. I want a city we can be proud of again. Not someday. Now.”

A detailed backgrounder follows.

text:
The public square at Yonge and Dundas is the busiest gathering place in the country. It is ringed by the Eaton Centre, the Ed Mirvish Theatre and Massey Hall, and it sits above a major transit hub. For years the space has struggled with cleanliness and safety, including visible drug use, and with a growing sense among residents and visitors that it has been allowed to decline. The plan treats that decline as fixable, not permanent.

The plan, in three parts

1. Clean and safe. Published cleaning and maintenance standards, so the public bar is clear and the City has to meet it. A steady safety presence, including looking to establish a permanent police substation staffed by officers already on the force. Expanded outreach, mental health support and housing for people in crisis in and around the square.

2. Alive again. A year-round programming calendar of commerce, culture, food, retail and live performance, developed with the surrounding businesses and the Business Improvement Area to draw families back.

3. A tribute to our story. The square’s permanent digital screens would carry a rotating tribute to celebrated Canadians between events and advertising.

• Terry Fox: his 1980 Marathon of Hope made him the country’s most enduring symbol of courage and a lasting inspiration for cancer research.

• Tom Longboat: Onondaga distance runner from Six Nations, winner of the 1907 Boston Marathon and a Toronto sporting legend.

• Sir Frederick Banting: co-discoverer of insulin at the University of Toronto and a Nobel laureate whose work has saved millions of lives.

• Lucie and Thornton Blackburn: owned Toronto’s first cab company, built homes for newcomers and were community activists who lived near today’s Distillery District.

Process and governance

"The people of Scarborough have been overlooked by Mayor Chow for long enough," says Bradford, pledging a personal funding push to Queen's Park and Ottawa in his first 100 days and shovels in the ground by the end of the term

TORONTO, ON | Standing outside the University of Toronto Scarborough Campus this morning, Brad Bradford made his commitment to Scarborough plain: when he's mayor, the Eglinton East LRT is his top transit priority, backed by a funding mission to Queen's Park and Ottawa in his first 100 days and a commitment to get shovels in the ground before the end of his first term.

Every day, hundreds of thousands of Scarborough residents pay the Olivia Chow Time Tax at a rate no other part of Toronto would accept. Students at the University of Toronto Scarborough spend upwards of two hours getting to a campus that should be twenty minutes away. Workers from Malvern heading to a job or a hospital shift ride a system that has quietly trained them to expect less. The Eglinton East LRT is the project that changes that, and it has been waiting more than a decade for a mayor willing to fight for it.
doc_title: BRADFORD: "WHEN I'M MAYOR, THE EGLINTON EAST LRT IS MY TOP TRANSIT PRIORITY"

text:
"When I'm mayor, this is my top transit priority," said Bradford. "The people of Scarborough have been overlooked by this mayor for long enough. The plan exists. The route is drawn. The environmental assessment is done. What's missing is a mayor who fights for this line the way City Hall has always fought for downtown. That's the change I'm offering, and I'll start by taking Scarborough's case to Queen's Park and Ottawa myself, in my first 100 days."

The Eglinton East LRT is an 18.6-kilometre line from Kennedy Station through eastern Scarborough to Malvern Town Centre, with 27 stops serving UTSC, Centennial College and eight Neighbourhood Improvement Areas. The city has put roughly $1.2 billion on the table toward the $4.65-billion project. The province has committed nothing, and in April the provincial Transportation Minister said the line is "a municipally-led project" that is not on the province's priority list. The federal government has committed nothing. There is no construction date.
doc_title: BRADFORD: "WHEN I'M MAYOR, THE EGLINTON EAST LRT IS MY TOP TRANSIT PRIORITY"

text:
This spring, after Bradford forced the issue at City Council, NDP Mayor Olivia Chow responded. She gave the project a new name, the Scarborough East Rapid Transit line, declared it the city's top transit priority, added $10 million for design work, and struck a working group. Five months later, not one senior government dollar has been committed and no construction date exists. The downtown waterfront LRT, which was advanced by unanimous Council vote in June 2022 as an equal pair with Scarborough's line, received $3 billion in committed three-way funding in March. Scarborough received a rebrand.

"A new name is not a transit line. A working group is not a shovel. Scarborough can't ride a rename," said Bradford. "The downtown waterfront got the Prime Minister, the Premier and three billion dollars. Scarborough got a press release. That's just how it is in Olivia Chow's Toronto, and it doesn't have to be."
doc_title: BRADFORD: "WHEN I'M MAYOR, THE EGLINTON EAST LRT IS MY TOP TRANSIT PRIORITY"

text:
At the end of this month, the Mayor will open the Scarborough Busway, conveniently just in time for an election. Bradford supports the busway as what it was always meant to be: a bridge. As mayor, he will make sure it stays a bridge and not a destination, by tying it publicly to a construction start date for the LRT it was built to precede.

As mayor, Bradford will make the Eglinton East LRT Toronto's top transit priority in action, not in name. He will personally lead Toronto's funding case to the provincial and federal governments in his first 100 days, making the ask respectfully, across the table, with a business case that serves eight Neighbourhood Improvement Areas, two post-secondary campuses and tens of thousands of transit-dependent residents. He will get shovels in the ground by 2030, the end of the next Council term. And he will fight for a Kennedy Station connection done right, so riders get a fast, seamless link to the rest of the network.
doc_title: BRADFORD: "WHEN I'M MAYOR, THE EGLINTON EAST LRT IS MY TOP TRANSIT PRIORITY"

And nowhere is it more stuck than on a bus in Scarborough. A stuck city only gets moving one way, and that's change. On October 26th, Scarborough can choose change. Not later. Right now."

text:
At tonight's Toronto Region Board of Trade debate, Bradford commits to a one-year freeze and the first independent, line by line review of city spending since 2011

TORONTO, ON | At tonight's Toronto Region Board of Trade mayoral debate, Brad Bradford announced that as mayor he will freeze property taxes for one year, for homes and businesses alike, while an independent, line by line review finds out where Torontonians' money is actually going.

Right now, nobody can answer that question. The City of Toronto hasn't had an independent, line by line look at its spending since 2011. In the 15 years since, the city's operating budget has grown by billions of dollars. The Mayor doesn’t care. She doesn’t think it’s important because in her view, this is as good as it gets. Toronto has reached its full potential. Brad Bradford rejects that idea. But this isn’t the first time Bradford and Chow see things differently.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL FREEZE PROPERTY TAXES FOR ONE YEAR WHILE WE FIND WHERE THE BILLIONS WENT.

text:
In 2023, Olivia Chow promised property tax increases would be "modest." Then she delivered a 9.5 per cent increase, then a 6.9 per cent increase, then an election-year 2.2 per cent increase she only got that low by drawing $1.7 billion from the city's reserves. That's nearly 20 per cent compounded, almost $700 more a year on the average home.

It happened while the province sent Toronto more help than ever before. The 2023 New Deal is worth roughly $9 billion to the city over 10 years, including taking the Gardiner Expressway and the Don Valley Parkway off the city's books. More money than ever, higher taxes than ever, and a city that works worse than ever. Food bank visits hit a record 4.1 million last year, up 340 per cent since 2019. Torontonians sit through the worst commutes in North America. Where did the money go?

Now the Mayor is promising to hold increases to “around” the rate of inflation. She promised "modest" last time too.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL FREEZE PROPERTY TAXES FOR ONE YEAR WHILE WE FIND WHERE THE BILLIONS WENT.

text:
"Every family in this city has had to sit down at the kitchen table and figure out exactly where their money goes. City Hall should have to do the same," said Bradford. "Olivia Chow has raised your property taxes nearly 20 per cent and she still can't tell you where the money went. So we're going to stop. No more increases until we open the books, read every line, and show Torontonians what we find."

The freeze is already paid for. A 2 per cent property tax increase raises about $100 million, and City Hall already has that room. It has it every year. In 2025, for the part of the budget that property taxes pay for, the city budgeted about $5.6 billion and spent about $5.5 billion, $100 million less than it planned. In 2024, that gap was $130 million.

Every year, City Hall sets your property taxes as if it will spend every dollar it budgets. Every year, it doesn't. Bradford's fiscal plan budgets for what the city actually spends and uses about $100 million of that recurring room to pay for the freeze. That means no property tax increase and no cuts to front-line services that people depend on.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL FREEZE PROPERTY TAXES FOR ONE YEAR WHILE WE FIND WHERE THE BILLIONS WENT.

text:
"City Hall is taxing you for money it doesn't even spend," said Bradford. "Everyone in this room knows no business would go 15 years without an audit, and no business would survive budgeting like this. That's not a revenue problem. That's a management problem."

The freeze covers the City Tax Rate of every property in the city, homes and businesses alike. Toronto is competing with every major city in North America for jobs and investment, and the businesses that employ Torontonians have been paying more and getting less too. A year of certainty on property taxes tells every employer in this city that City Hall is finally getting its own house in order.

The line-by-line review will be led by an independent group of experts and former city leaders and will cover every division, agency and program. The goal is to protect and improve frontline services while finding the waste, the duplication and the outdated programs. Once the review is done, any future property tax increase will be kept below the rate of inflation.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL FREEZE PROPERTY TAXES FOR ONE YEAR WHILE WE FIND WHERE THE BILLIONS WENT.

text: "The Mayor says Toronto is living up to its full potential. I don't accept that. We're not even close," said Bradford. "Toronto isn't broken. It's stuck. And stuck is a choice. On October 26, Torontonians can choose change: a city that's safe, a city you can afford, a city that moves. A Toronto we can be proud of."

text:
Mayoral candidate Brad Bradford calls for motor-style e-bikes to be licensed and insured as part of eight-point public safety package

TORONTO. City Councillor and mayoral candidate Brad Bradford today released a comprehensive proposal targeting the growing threat of motor-style, out-of-class electric bikes on Toronto streets, sidewalks, cycle tracks, and in residential buildings.

Bradford's plan is part of his commitment to make Toronto a city we can be proud of again: a city that is safe for pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists, and one that takes congestion seriously.

A growing class of two-wheeled electric mini-motorcycles, many of them styled as sport bikes, are being operated on Toronto streets, sidewalks, cycle tracks, and multi-use trails without licences, insurance, or plates.

The core of the proposal would ensure that these mini-motorcycles are licensed and insured, as any other motor vehicle on our roadways would be. Bradford’s plan also calls for police to be given the power to seize and impound illegally modified e-bikes.
doc_title: BRADFORD DECLARES CRACKDOWN ON DANGEROUS E-BIKES

text:
The danger is not only on Toronto streets. It is in Toronto homes. Toronto Fire Services has reported a substantial year-over-year increase in lithium-ion battery fires associated with personal mobility devices in residential buildings.

“A pedal welded to a mini motorcycle does not make it a bicycle. A senior on the sidewalk, a parent in the bike lane, and a family in an apartment building deserve more than a City Hall that has chosen willful ignorance over leadership. As Mayor, I will use every tool the City already has, and I will work in good faith with the Province and Ottawa, so that public safety in this city means something again.”

— Brad Bradford

While Council will deliberate on an open provincial consultation this week and has asked City staff to return with by-law amendments by January 2027, Torontonians deserve a council and a mayor who take action now.

The eight-point package combines actions the City can take today under its existing authority with targeted requests of the Province of Ontario and the federal government.
doc_title: BRADFORD DECLARES CRACKDOWN ON DANGEROUS E-BIKES

text:
“Under Mayor Chow, we have been asked to accept that motorcycles on the sidewalk and battery fires in our buildings are just the price of a growing city. They are not. Innovation does not have to come at the cost of public safety. Toronto deserves a mayor who addresses these concerns, not one who waits for someone else to do it. That is not leadership.”

— Brad Bradford

BACKGROUND

Under Ontario's Highway Traffic Act and O. Reg. 369/09, a lawful power-assisted bicycle must meet strict criteria: functional pedals, a motor of 500 watts or less, a 32 km/h speed cut-off, a maximum unladen weight of 120 kg, and certified brakes. Devices that fail any of those tests are not lawful e-bikes. Many are nonetheless sold, modified and operated on our streets.

Toronto Fire Services has reported a substantial year-over-year increase in lithium-ion battery fires associated with personal mobility devices in residential buildings. The Province has opened ERO Posting 026-0422 for public comment until June 7, 2026. Toronto City Council has directed staff to return with by-law amendments in2027. Bradford argues the City cannot wait.

THE EIGHT-POINT PACKAGE
doc_title: BRADFORD DECLARES CRACKDOWN ON DANGEROUS E-BIKES

text:
-
Fast-track changes to the Toronto Municipal Code to ban mini-motorcycles and other motorized vehicles in bike lanes, cycle tracks, painted lanes, and multi-use trails.

-
Call on the Province to amend the Highway Traffic Act to authorize Toronto Police and designated by-law officers to seize and impound illegally modified out-of-class motorized devices at the curb.

-
Request courier and transportation businesses operating in Toronto to educate contractors on the penalties associated with illegal modifications to e-bikes and the requirement to comply with all rules of the road.

-
Recommend the Province adopt the two-class e-bike definition and add an appearance-based exclusion, modelled on Quebec's Highway Safety Code, that disqualifies motorcycle and moped-styled devices regardless of label, based on visible features such as footrests, body panels, non-adjustable saddles, and motorcycle-style wheels.

-
Stand up a Toronto E-Bike Safety Task Force, jointly led by Toronto Fire Services and Municipal Licensing and Standards, with authority to inspect retailers, publish quarterly safety data, and suspend or revoke licences for repeat violators.
doc_title: BRADFORD DECLARES CRACKDOWN ON DANGEROUS E-BIKES

text:
-
Require a Toronto Safe Riding point-of-sale notice as a binding condition of e-bike retailer licensing, turning an existing education recommendation into an enforceable obligation.

-
Request the Province mandate top-tier safety certification (UL 2849 and UL 2271) for e-bike electrical systems and batteries sold in Ontario.

-
Call on the federal government to set mandatory lithium-ion battery safety standards for imported e-bikes, e-scooters, and their batteries and chargers under the Canada Consumer Product Safety Act, and to give the Canada Border Services Agency clear authority and the tools it needs to detain and refuse non-compliant shipments at the border.

text:
Bike lanes belong on residential side streets and in parks, hydro corridors and ravines, not squeezed onto Etobicoke's main street

TORONTO, ON | As part of his plan to alleviate congestion in Toronto, Brad Bradford committed that as Mayor he will remove the bike lanes on Bloor Street West from South Kingsway west to Resurrection Road, restore the traffic lanes, and direct city staff to begin the work in his first year. The removal is paired with a plan to redirect the city's cycling investment into a network of residential streets and multi-use trails in parks, hydro corridors and ravines.

“People here in Etobicoke told City Hall exactly what these lanes would do to their main street, and City Hall didn't listen,” said Bradford. “Commuters in Etobicoke have seen with their own eyes, every day for two years, the congestion and chaos that they have created. Within my first year in office as your Mayor, these lanes are coming out, the traffic lanes are going back in, and that is my commitment. Not another review.”
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL REMOVE ETOBICOKE BLOOR ST. W BIKE LANES  AND BUILD A CITYWIDE NETWORK FOR CYCLISTS

text:
The lanes were installed in 2023 and 2024 against overwhelming objections from local residents and businesses. In February 2025, more than 40 local businesses filed a $10 million lawsuit against the City of Toronto over the lanes and the consultation process that produced them.

“City Hall needs to have the humility to acknowledge when something isn’t working, and to go back and fix it. These bike lanes in Etobicoke aren’t working,” said Bradford.

Bradford's plan, Build Bike Lanes Where They Belong, will:

-
Create an integrated network of residential streets and multi-use trails in parks, hydro corridors and ravines that gives cyclists a safer, faster alternative to riding on arterial roads.

-
Properly maintain key trails through the winter so they are safe and usable year round.

-
Complete the trail and connector projects that have languished in municipal plans for fifteen years, including the 81 kilometre Loop Trail and the Meadoway in Scarborough.

-
Finish the West Toronto Railpath at a responsible cost, after the current extension's price tag climbed toward $200 million.
doc_title: BRADFORD WILL REMOVE ETOBICOKE BLOOR ST. W BIKE LANES  AND BUILD A CITYWIDE NETWORK FOR CYCLISTS

text:
“I'm a city planner and a cyclist. I want more people on bikes in this city, not fewer. I also want less congestion, and for everyone to make it home safely and on time,” said Bradford. “Toronto is sitting on the largest ravine system in the world and hydro corridors that run for kilometres in every direction. And our residential neighbourhoods have quiet, welcoming streets. Build the network there, keep it plowed in the winter, and everybody gets what they actually want. Cyclists ride without fighting trucks for space, drivers get their lanes back, and businesses get their customers back.”

For nearly two years, decisions about Toronto's bike lanes have been fought between City Hall and Queen's Park in the courts, at a cost to taxpayers and with no resolution for the street. The province's Bill 212 ordered the removal of the Bloor, Yonge and University bike lanes in November 2024; the Superior Court ruled the forced removal unconstitutional in July 2025; and the province's appeal was heard by the Court of Appeal in January 2026, with a decision still pending.

“Toronto's streets should be planned by Toronto, with the voices of Toronto residents,” said Bradford. “When the city gets this right itself, Queen's Park doesn't need to reach into our streets at all.”

Bradford will pursue federal partnership for the trail network, including active transportation and climate adaptation funding programs.

text:
Last updated Oct 20, 2026

Summary

Brad Bradford, candidate for Mayor of Toronto in the October 26, 2026 municipal election, has published a cost and a funding source for each of his five major commitments. Only one of the five, hiring 1,000 front-line police officers, is new ongoing spending. It phases in over four years and reaches about $143 million a year at full strength.

The other four are funded from money the City of Toronto already collects or already budgets. The one-year property tax freeze (about $100 million) is paid for from recurring operating underspend. The municipal land transfer tax exemption (about $300 million a year) is paid for by ending the practice of pre-paying capital projects out of operating revenue, plus a water utility dividend. The 25% water bill cut ends an overcharge of roughly $400 million a year. The TTC money-back guarantee is estimated at $3.5 million to $7 million a year.

The plan does not use borrowing for operating costs. The operating budget balances every year, as Ontario's Municipal Act requires. Borrowing is limited to capital assets, under two new caps on debt costs.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
All figures come from City of Toronto budget documents, the City's year-end variance reports, the 2024 Financial Information Return and the Toronto Police Service 2026 budget. Sources are listed at the end of this page.

Key figures at a glance

-
One-year property tax freeze: about $100 million, one time. Funded from the City's recurring operating underspend (about $100 million in 2025, about $130 million in 2024).

-
Municipal land transfer tax exemption: about $300 million a year in forgone revenue. Funded from operating-to-capital transfers already in the City's 2026 budget ($256 million in 2027, $369 million in 2028), plus a water utility dividend (about $45 million in 2027, building toward about $125 million).

-
25% water bill cut: not a cost to taxpayers. In 2024 the water system cost $909 million to run and billed $1.32 billion.

-
TTC money-back guarantee: about $3.5 million to $7 million a year, or 0.3% to 0.7% of fare revenue.

-
1,000 front-line police officers: about $36 million in year one, rising to about $143 million a year by year four.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
-
New debt rules: interest never above 4 cents per dollar of City revenue, and total debt costs never above 10% of own-source revenue. No borrowing for operating costs.

How does Brad Bradford pay for the property tax freeze?

The one-year freeze on the base City tax levy costs about $100 million, and it is paid for from money the City budgets each year but does not spend. A 2% increase, which covers normal inflation, raises roughly $100 million. That is the cost of not raising it.

The City's own year-end Operating Variance Reports show this underspend recurs. In 2025, on the property-tax-supported part of the operating budget, the City budgeted about $5.64 billion and spent about $5.54 billion, leaving close to $100 million. In 2024 the figure was about $130 million.

The underspend is structural. The City budgets every approved position at full cost whether or not it is filled, then sets property taxes as if every dollar will be spent. Mayor Olivia Chow's 2026 budget relies on the same money: it balances with $323 million of budget bridging from reserves and the 2025 surplus.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
The freeze covers homes and businesses for one year, while an independent line-by-line review of City spending takes place. After that year, Brad Bradford has committed to keep increases below inflation. The freeze applies to the base City levy, not the separate City Building Fund levy, which has risen 1.5% a year since 2020 and supports long-term infrastructure financing.

How does Brad Bradford pay for cutting Toronto's land transfer tax?

The exemption costs about $300 million a year in forgone revenue, and both funding sources appear in the City's own 2026 Budget Summary. Toronto collects about $850 million a year from its municipal land transfer tax, forecast to rise to $923 million and then $988 million.

Who qualifies: first-time buyers, and Toronto homeowners selling one principal residence to buy another. The tax is eliminated on the value of the home below the previous year's average Toronto resale price, which was $1.1 million for 2025. Value above that threshold is still taxed. The December 2025 rates on homes over $3 million stay in place. Investors and landlords with more than one property (29% of purchases), corporations and commercial buyers continue to pay in full.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
What it saves: on a $1.1 million home, the municipal land transfer tax is about $18,000. The current first-time buyer rebate has been fixed at the tax on a $400,000 home since 2008 and fully exempts about 2.6% of homes. The new threshold covers up to two thirds of resale homes.

Funding source one is the operating revenue the City already plans to move into the capital budget. The 2026 Budget Summary earmarks $130 million of land transfer tax revenue in 2027 and $195 million in 2028 for capital (page 265), plus $126 million in 2027 and $174 million in 2028 of general revenue as "capital from current" (page 263). That totals about $256 million in 2027 and $369 million in 2028. The plan stops these transfers and finances the same capital over the life of each asset instead, as the federal government, every province and Toronto Hydro already do.

Funding source two is a dividend from a publicly owned water utility: about $45 million in 2027 while the utility is set up, building toward about $125 million at maturity. For comparison, Winnipeg's water utility pays its city a dividend of 10% of revenue.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
In 2027 the transfers plus the dividend cover the $300 million. From 2028 the transfers alone exceed it. The dividend is a backstop if land transfer tax revenue falls in a weak housing market. No project in the capital plan is cut; what changes is when and how it is paid for.

Why is the 25% water bill cut not a cost to taxpayers?

The water bill cut is not new spending; it ends an overcharge. In 2024 Toronto's water and wastewater system cost $909 million to run, including amortization, and billed users $1.32 billion. That is roughly $400 million a year collected beyond the cost of running the system, and 2025 was similar.

The cut is about $300 a year for the average household, whose 2026 bill is $1,118. Today 67 cents of every water dollar goes to capital rather than delivering water. The water capital reserve has grown from $141 million in 2009 to about $2 billion, losing purchasing power to inflation. Toronto Water carries no debt and underspent its 2025 budget by nearly $400 million.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
Under the plan, water becomes a City-owned utility run like Toronto Hydro. It borrows against pipes and plants that last 50 to 100 years and recovers the cost over their life, instead of collecting the cash up front. Savings are capped for bills above $1,500 a year, so the cut is focused on residents rather than large commercial, institutional and industrial users.

Ownership stays 100% public, protected three ways: Brad Bradford's commitment, a City bylaw permanently barring private investment, and Ontario's Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025, as amended by Bill 98 in May 2026, which restricts shares to a municipality, the Province, the Government of Canada or their agents. Edmonton, Windsor, Kingston and Halifax already run water this way, and Peel Region is moving to it.

What does the TTC money-back guarantee cost?

The guarantee is estimated to cost $3.5 million to $7 million a year, or 0.3% to 0.7% of TTC fare revenue. Riders whose trip is delayed 15 minutes or more get a refund or credit. The TTC designs the details, with exceptions for events outside its control such as extreme weather.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
The estimate is based on experience elsewhere. GO Transit has offered a service guarantee since 2012, and London, Singapore and Washington, D.C. run similar programs. On Washington's WMATA system, about 0.3% of trips received a refund. The TTC carried about 420 million trips in 2024 and collected roughly $1.0 billion in fares. If about 0.5% of trips receive a credit, the cost falls in the range above. If claims run higher, caps can be tightened.

No new fare gates are needed. Riders submit their trip details, and a refund is issued when the claim matches TTC operating records. The TTC controls the cost by running on time, which makes the guarantee an accountability tool rather than a significant budget line.

What would 1,000 new police officers cost?

Hiring 1,000 front-line officers would cost about $143 million a year at full strength, reached in year four. This is the one commitment that adds new ongoing spending, and Brad Bradford has said so since he announced it.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
The arithmetic uses the City's own numbers. The Toronto Police Service 2026 budget allocates $20.5 million to hire 143 new officers, about $143,000 per officer fully loaded. Hiring roughly 250 officers a year costs about $36 million in year one, rising to about $143 million in year four. Costs grow as recruits move up the constable pay grid, which is why hiring is phased over a full term. Councillor Shelley Carroll's estimate of "well over $100 million" is consistent with this figure.

For scale, the police budget is about $1.43 billion and rose about $94 million, roughly 7%, in 2026 alone. That increase came in a year when Mayor Chow's budget held the operating property tax increase to 0.7%. At full strength the commitment equals about 10% of today's police budget, reached over four years, and can be managed through the annual budget process.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
Why 1,000: Toronto's population has grown 21% since 2010, about half a million people, with about the same number of deployed officers. The Police Services Board's hiring plan, approved December 12, 2024, takes deployed strength from 5,433 to 5,935 by 2029, or 172 officers per 100,000 residents. Montreal has 221, Vancouver 196, Edmonton 188 and Winnipeg 186. The current plan adds only about 250 officers during the next council term; the 1,000 officers would be on patrol, in neighbourhoods and at subway stations.

Does Brad Bradford's platform cost $6 billion?

No. The $6 billion figure was produced by Mayor Olivia Chow's campaign on October 1, 2026, without published calculations. Adding the costs above gives a total far below it: about $100 million once for the freeze, about $300 million a year for the land transfer tax, $3.5 million to $7 million a year for the TTC guarantee, and up to $143 million a year for police.

The only way to approach $6 billion is to count capital projects, such as platform edge doors, as new operating spending. These are long-lived assets financed over their life, the same way Toronto Hydro and every Canadian province finance infrastructure.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
What happens if the line-by-line review finds less than expected?

Nothing in the plan depends on the review finding a specific number. Each commitment has its own funding source, listed above, and Brad Bradford has not promised a savings target from the review.

The review's purpose is to look for waste, duplication and programs that have outlived their purpose, not to cut front-line services. Toronto's operating budget was about $9 billion at the last comprehensive review in 2011 and is over $18 billion today. Examples of the waste it would target include $11 million the Auditor General found spent on software licences for people who no longer work for the City.

Brad Bradford: "I'm a city planner by training. When something isn't working, you don't guess. You look under the hood. We're on the cusp of change in this city, and change starts with knowing where the money went."

How have Toronto's finances changed since 2023?

Toronto's operating budget rose from $16.16 billion in 2023 to $18.9 billion in 2026, an increase of $2.7 billion or about 17% in three years. The 10-year capital plan is a record $63.1 billion.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
Residential property taxes rose 9.5% in 2024, 6.9% in 2025 and 2.2% in 2026, nearly 20% compounded, or almost $700 a year on the average home. The 2024 increase was the largest in the city's history.

The spending growth has not closed the City's structural gap. The 2024 budget opened with about $1.8 billion in pressures, and the City's 2026 Budget Summary projects a $1.6 billion gap for 2027 (page 14). This came alongside new provincial support under the November 2023 Ontario-Toronto New Deal, including the upload of the Gardiner Expressway and Don Valley Parkway.

Over the same period, food bank visits in Toronto reached 4.1 million, up 340% since 2019, according to Daily Bread Food Bank and North York Harvest.

Frequently asked questions

Which commitment adds new spending? Only the 1,000 police officers, at about $143 million a year by year four.

Is the property tax freeze permanent? No. It is a one-year freeze on the base City levy. After that, increases are committed to stay below inflation.
doc_title: How Brad Bradford Pays for His Platform: Toronto 2026 Fiscal Plan Explained

text:
Does the freeze include the City Building Fund levy? No. The City Building Fund levy is separate and supports long-term infrastructure financing.

Is the underspend that funds the freeze one-time money? No. The City underspent its tax-supported operating budget by about $130 million in 2024 and about $100 million in 2025, and the current budget itself relies on prior-year surplus.

Will the water utility be privatized? No. Provincial law as amended in May 2026 restricts shares to public governments, and a City bylaw would permanently bar private investment.

Will the City borrow to pay operating costs? No. Borrowing is limited to capital, and the operating budget must balance every year under the Municipal Act.

What if land transfer tax revenue drops? The water utility dividend is a backstop, and from 2028 the operating-to-capital transfers alone exceed the $300 million cost.

Does the plan depend on savings from the line-by-line review? No. None of the commitments is funded by the review.

7 trucks that deliver rescued food to charities across the city are out of service after catalytic converters were stolen over the Thanksgiving weekend. Donate at secondharvest.ca.

TORONTO, ON | Brad Bradford visited Second Harvest's truck yard in Etobicoke today, where 7 of the charity's delivery trucks sit idle after thieves cut a hole through the fence over the Thanksgiving weekend and stole the catalytic converters from under them. The break-in took minutes. The repairs will take 2 to 3 weeks and cost about $80,000, money that was meant to go to rescuing good food and getting it to people who need it.

Second Harvest is Canada's largest food rescue organization. Its trucks collect surplus food from grocers, producers and distributors and deliver it to more than 500 charities across Toronto, from food banks and shelters to school programs and seniors' centres.

It's the second time this year the fleet has been targeted. On New Year's Day, four trucks were sabotaged and taken out of service.
doc_title: THIEVES HIT A FOOD CHARITY TWICE IN ONE YEAR. BRADFORD CALLS ON TORONTO TO HELP SECOND HARVEST

text:
"This is a charity that feeds people, and someone crawled under its trucks in the middle of the night and took them off the road," said Bradford. "Food bank visits in Toronto are up 340% since 2019. There were 4.1 million visits last year alone. The food on these trucks was headed to the people behind those numbers. They're the ones who got robbed this weekend."

Bradford said the theft reflects a pattern residents across the city recognize. Homicides and shootings are down this year, and the credit belongs to the men and women of the Toronto Police Service. But auto theft, break and enters, thefts over $5,000 and major crime overall are up in 2026, according to the Toronto Police Service's own numbers.

"Catalytic converters, stolen cars, kicked-in doors, smashed storefronts. These get called small crimes, and they aren't small to the people on the receiving end," said Bradford. "Somewhere along the way this city got used to it. I don't accept that. A charity feeding hungry people shouldn't have to budget for thieves. A city that is not safe is not free."

Today, Bradford's ask is simpler: help Second Harvest get its trucks moving again.

"Second Harvest has been a lifeline for this city for decades, and right now it needs one back," said Bradford. "Every dollar donated goes to repairing these trucks and getting food to the charities counting on them. Toronto isn't broken. It's stuck. And the way we get unstuck is by looking after each other. text:
Summary

Under Brad Bradford's water plan, Toronto's water system stays 100% publicly owned. Ontario law allows shares in a municipal water corporation to be held only by a municipality, the Province of Ontario, the Government of Canada or an agent of one of them. A Toronto bylaw would also bar private investment of any kind, and the City of Toronto would be the sole shareholder.

Brad Bradford, candidate for Mayor of Toronto in the October 26, 2026 election, proposes moving Toronto Water into a City-owned utility, run the way Toronto Hydro has been run since 1999. The plan cuts water bills by 25%, about $300 a year for the average household, with no service cuts - as explained in the September 28 release.

Mayor Olivia Chow's campaign has described the plan as privatization. The law, the bylaw and the ownership structure all say otherwise. The Bradford campaign's view is that the claim is meant to shift attention away from Toronto's rising water bills and the roughly $2 billion in reserves collected from residents.

What does Brad Bradford's water plan do?
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
The plan cuts every Toronto water bill by 25% on the first $1,500 of charges, about $300 a year for the average household. The cut is automatic, with no application, and no water services are reduced.

Today the average household pays $1,118 a year for water and wastewater, according to the City's 2026 Water and Wastewater Rate Budget. That bill is up 75% since 2009 and has risen in each of the last three years. About two thirds of each bill goes to capital rather than to delivering water.

In 2024 the system cost $909 million to run, including amortization, and billed $1.32 billion. The water reserves have grown from $141 million in 2009 to about $2 billion, and Toronto Water underspent its 2025 budget by nearly $400 million. The cut is paid for by ending this overcharge, not by raising other taxes.

How the utility would work:

-
The City of Toronto is the sole shareholder.

-
Rates are set by an independent, skills-based board appointed by City Council, within guidance set by Council.

-
The utility borrows to build long-lived pipes and plants and recovers the cost over their 50- to 100-year life, instead of collecting it all up front.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
-
Toronto Water employees keep the same jobs under the same contracts; existing collective agreements carry over under the provincial framework.

-
Brad Bradford has written to Ontario's Minister of Municipal Affairs and Housing, Rob Flack, asking that the Residential Tenancies Act rent-reduction mechanism cover water rate cuts, so renters benefit too.

Can Toronto's water utility be privatized under Brad Bradford's plan?

No. Three separate protections keep Toronto's water utility in public hands, and each would have to fail for private ownership to happen. It would be 100% public, by law and by bylaw.

-
Provincial law. Section 9 of Ontario's Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025 says shares of a water corporation cannot be issued to anyone other than a municipality, the Province of Ontario, the Government of Canada or an agent of one of them. Existing shareholders cannot sell or transfer shares to anyone else. Bill 98, passed May 14, 2026, added these limits to guarantee 100% public ownership.

-
City bylaw. Brad Bradford has committed to a Toronto bylaw barring private investment of any kind in the utility. Repealing it would take a public vote of City Council.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
-
Sole public shareholder. The City of Toronto owns 100% of the utility on behalf of Toronto taxpayers, as it owns Toronto Hydro.

Under the Act, core service assets cannot be sold off unless they are declared surplus. Water quality stays regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002, as it is today.

A private investor, pension fund or foreign company cannot buy shares in Toronto's water utility under this framework. Calling the plan privatization describes something the law does not allow.

Answers to the most common objections

"A future government could change the law." Any law can be amended, including the laws that govern Toronto Water today. Under the current system, water is a City department with no statutory ban on privatization at all. The utility model adds a provincial share restriction and a City bylaw that do not exist now. Privatizing it would take a new provincial law and a Council vote to repeal the bylaw, both in public.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
"The Act lets an 'agent' of government hold shares." Some municipalities have asked the Province to define "agent" more tightly. In Toronto the question does not arise: the City is the sole shareholder, and the City bylaw bars private investment of any kind.

"Highway 407 was public and then went private." The 407 was sold under a law that allowed its sale. The Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act expressly prohibits private ownership, so the same step would require changing the law first.

"A dividend to the City is just a hidden tax." Toronto Hydro has paid the City a dividend for decades without being called privatized. The water dividend is about $45 million in 2027, building toward about $125 million, while residents' bills fall by about $300 a year.

"Borrowing will drive rates up." Rates today include a large charge for pipes not yet built. Financing long-lived assets over their life lets today's bill reflect today's costs. Rates are set by a Council-appointed board within Council's guidance.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
"If the utility defaults, a lender could seize the pipes." Under the Act, core water and wastewater assets cannot be sold unless Council declares them surplus. The utility borrows the way Toronto Hydro has since 1999.

"The union's legal opinion says the City can't bind the Province." The opinion, commissioned by CUPE Local 416 from Goldblatt Partners, argues that no City bylaw can stop a future provincial law. That is true of every arrangement the City has, including Toronto Water today, which sits under provincial statute with no ban on privatization at all. The utility model adds a statutory share restriction and a City bylaw that do not exist now.

Where does this model already work?

Publicly owned utility corporations are a common way for Canadian cities to deliver water and power, and none of the examples below are privatized.

-
Toronto Hydro: owned by the City of Toronto since 1999. It borrows to build, charges what service costs and pays a dividend to the City.

-
EPCOR, Edmonton: 100% owned by the City of Edmonton.

-
Enwin Utilities, Windsor; Utilities Kingston; Halifax Water: publicly owned utilities delivering water.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
-
Peel Region: transitioning to a water and wastewater public corporation now, under the same provincial Act.

-
Calgary: an independent expert review panel recommended a utility model after the 2024 Bearspaw feeder main failure.

Describing Toronto's plan as privatization implies each of these cities sold its water. None of them did.

Why is Olivia Chow's campaign calling it privatization?

The Bradford campaign's view is that the privatization claim shifts the debate away from Toronto's water bills, which have risen every year of Mayor Chow's term. A debate about water rates puts the City's own numbers in front of voters.

Those numbers include:

-
An average household bill of $1,118 a year, up 75% since 2009.

-
About two thirds of each bill going to capital, much of it for pipes and plants not yet built.

-
Reserves of about $2 billion, up from $141 million in 2009, collected from residents through their water bills.

-
An underspend of nearly $400 million in Toronto Water's 2025 budget.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
Privatization is a powerful word in a water debate, and voters are right to care about it. That is why the facts matter: the provincial law, the City bylaw and the City's sole ownership all rule it out.

Brad Bradford: "It's a ridiculous attack from Mayor Chow's campaign which is out of ideas and out of gas. Under my plan, Toronto's water stays 100% publicly owned. Not 99%. Not public with an asterisk. 100%, by law and by bylaw."

Frequently asked questions

Is Brad Bradford privatizing Toronto's water? No. The utility would be 100% owned by the City of Toronto, and Ontario law limits ownership to governments.

Who could own shares in the utility? Only a municipality, the Province of Ontario, the Government of Canada or an agent of one of them, under section 9 of the Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025. In Toronto, the City would be the only shareholder.

Could the City sell the utility later? Not to a private buyer under current law. Shares can only be transferred to another government, and a City bylaw would bar private investment.

How much would my water bill drop? About 25% on the first $1,500 of charges, roughly $300 a year for the average household.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
Do renters benefit? Brad Bradford has asked the Province to extend the Residential Tenancies Act rent-reduction mechanism to water rate cuts so renters see the savings.

What happens to Toronto Water employees? They keep their jobs under the same contracts and collective agreements.

Who sets water rates? An independent, skills-based board appointed by City Council, working within guidance set by Council.
Is the board unelected and unaccountable? The board is appointed by City Council, works within guidance Council sets, and can be replaced by Council. Toronto Hydro, the TTC and Toronto Community Housing are governed the same way today.

Will Doug Ford control Toronto's water rates? No. Under the Water and Wastewater Public Corporations Act, 2025, setting rates is a duty of the water corporation itself. In Toronto that means a board appointed by City Council, working within guidance set by Council, with the City as sole shareholder. The Province sets the legal framework and regulations for water utilities, as it already does for Toronto Water today.
doc_title: Toronto's Water Stays Public: Brad Bradford's Water Plan Explained

text:
Will Toronto's water safety be put at risk? No. The same provincial safety laws that protect Toronto's drinking water today continue to apply, including the Safe Drinking Water Act, 2002 and the Ontario Water Resources Act. The same treatment plants, standards, inspections and Toronto Water staff stay in place. Financing pipes and plants over their life also lets the utility repair and replace ageing infrastructure sooner, instead of waiting until the cash is saved.

Is this how Toronto Hydro works? Yes. Toronto Hydro has been a City-owned corporation since 1999 and pays a dividend to the City.

TORONTO (September 14, 2026) — Olivia Chow took the stage tonight in front of a packed room at the Daily Bread Food Bank for the first mayoral debate of the campaign. She delivered a clear message: Toronto has turned a corner, and now is the time to keep moving forward, not go backwards. Torontonians saw a strong, poised Mayor, the same steady leadership that has guided City Hall through difficult times. In the face of uncertainty, Chow made clear that steady leadership, not chaos or division, is what Toronto needs right now.
doc_title: Olivia Chow brings her vision for Toronto to first mayoral debate - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
Chow laid out her record of making Toronto more affordable, more caring, and safer: expanding school food programs now reaching 330,000 kids and saving families up to $900 a year, speeding up 911 response times, and investing in frontline workers and youth. She reminded Torontonians that when she took office, TTC fares were rising and service was falling. She did the opposite: freezing fares and boosting service for transit riders.

Chow also spoke to standing up for Toronto families, from cracking down on bad landlords to stopping grocery giants from price gouging shoppers, and pointed to ending over a decade of stalled affordable housing construction. She highlighted her track record working with other levels of government, citing the confidence she's earned from Prime Minister Carney and Premier Doug Ford, while making clear she's never been afraid to stand up for the city when needed.

She drew a clear contrast with her opponents, pointing to her decades long fight for programs like school food since her time as a city councillor and MP, work she has now delivered as Mayor. Others on the stage struggled to point to anything they'd delivered for Torontonians.

SCARBOROUGH — Olivia Chow’s housing plan is getting rental homes built and supporting nearly 40,000 jobs in Scarborough and across Toronto.

Joined by Jason Ottey of LIUNA Local 183 at 26 Gilder Drive, Chow said support for rental construction helps keep skilled tradespeople working while building homes people need.

“When we get housing moving, we get people working. Here in Scarborough and across our city, that means a paycheque that covers rent, buys groceries and helps a family get ahead,” said Chow. “Our affordable housing projects support almost 40,000 jobs. These are livelihoods. These are families.”

doc_title: Olivia Chow kicks off re-election campaign – Speech and Recap - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
See below for Olivia Chow’s Rally Speech:

Toronto – are you ready to choose hope over fear? Unity over division? To move forward not backward? Are you ready to win?

I love Toronto! I love the vibrancy and energy from the millions of people who come to our street festivals – from all over the world. From every culture, heritage and language.

I love skating. I learned to skate at Nathan Phillips Square. It made me feel like a Canadian, like I belonged here. I loved that it was, and still is, free.

I learned how to ride a bike on Centre Island. I spent a lot of time at the Reference Library. I used old art books to build up my career as a struggling artist.

I love kayaking on our lake. It will always be Lake Ontario!

Our city made me who I am today. An immigrant kid from St Jamestown who became your mayor. And all of my best memories of our city happened in public spaces. Places we all created together.

All of the opportunities I had growing up happened because our city made them possible. Public spaces and services make our city great.

But today, we have challenges we need to solve, together.
doc_title: Olivia Chow kicks off re-election campaign – Speech and Recap - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
Far too many kids are lined up with their moms at the food bank. Too many go to bed hungry. Too many can’t concentrate at school because their bellies are empty and grumbling.

I remember the exact moment it became my mission to deal with child hunger. On a Christmas Eve 35 years ago, after dinner with my late husband Jack Layton and our family. We thought of all the children who would not have such an opportunity to have a holiday feast.

Together Jack and I dreamed about a plan to feed every kid in every school in Toronto. We calculated how much it would cost. We mapped out a detailed plan. We worked hard at City Hall to give children the best chance to be successful in life.

So it is with great joy, after 35 years, now as your mayor, finally, that program Jack and I dreamed of is a reality. In every classroom. In every school. For every child.

And we’re going to keep going. We are going to build more affordable housing. We are going to keep our streets safe. We are going to support public transit and make it even more affordable!
doc_title: Olivia Chow kicks off re-election campaign – Speech and Recap - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
All of these make our city better, stronger. They give every generation of kids and every family a chance. No matter if you’re from downtown, Scarborough, Etobicoke, North York, or any of the awesome neighbourhoods in our city.

When I first arrived at city hall as your mayor. No affordable housing was being built. That was a choice. I am making a different choice.

Today, thousands of new affordable homes are under construction. 7 out of 10 cranes in the sky are there because of the work we are doing.

When I first arrived at city hall three years ago, TTC riders were angry because their fares had gone up and their service had been cut.

That’s just not right.

As your mayor, I did the exact opposite. I kept the fares low, and I’m investing in faster service.

Back then, many libraries were closed on Sundays and evenings. Today, all 100 libraries are open 7 days a week with longer hours.

Back then, 911 wait times were well over the national average. Today, our city is safer. 911 call times are 90% faster. We have more first responders. Including mental health crisis workers city wide.
doc_title: Olivia Chow kicks off re-election campaign – Speech and Recap - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
Toronto, we have turned the corner, and we are feeling more optimistic. We have momentum. Now we have to keep that momentum going. Because these are not easy times. Trump and his tariffs create uncertainty and stress. Our world is rapidly changing around us. Everything is less affordable, for almost everyone..

So we have a choice to make.

We can choose to work together, support each other, continue building the city we love, a joyous city that invites us and welcomes us. Where we care for each other and stand up for each other.

Where we celebrate who we are: ambitious, hardworking, ready to win, ready to go forward. Where we build more housing and lower the cost of living. Where we decide our own future. As Torontonians.

Or we can go backwards. We could choose leaders who will starve our public spaces and cut our services. Divide us instead of bringing us together. That is not what I want. I do not believe it’s what you want either.

We love our city and we know we can build an even more caring, more affordable, and safer Toronto. Together.
doc_title: Olivia Chow kicks off re-election campaign – Speech and Recap - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
Where a mom shopping for groceries does not have to put anything back. Because our city is saving her money by feeding kids in school. Where you can count on public transit and fares are low, so more of us can be where we need to be.

Where slum lords no longer get a free ride, and are now fixing their long neglected buildings, so renters can live in dignity.

Where seniors can age in their home and their own neighbourhood.

Where your local government continues to lower your cost of living by building more affordable housing, faster.

Where grocery chains don’t rip you off by snooping on your shopping habits and raising the price.

We have built the foundation. Let’s finish what we started. Let’s choose to be confident and hopeful. Let’s choose to make our city more affordable. Let’s choose to care. Let’s choose to keep moving forward and keep building a Toronto we love, together.

TORONTO— Ahead of Thanksgiving, Olivia Chow announced her plan to lower grocery bills by banning surveillance pricing, cutting taxes for local grocers and bringing more stores closer to home.

Joined by families at Fresh Picked, a local independent grocery store, Chow said Toronto should use the tools at its disposal to bring costs down for families and protect shoppers from unfair pricing.

“People are paying more and more at the grocery store. In every corner of the city, people are asking if the City can help. They want and deserve a mayor that stands up for them,” said Chow. “I don’t want parents to make impossible choices at checkout because they can’t afford it. We have to use every power at our disposal to keep grocery prices fair and encourage more independent grocery stores to open, so we can give people more affordable options. That’s how we lower your grocery bill.”

Chow’s plan to Lower Your Grocery Bill will:

-
doc_title: Olivia Chow's Plan to Lower Your Grocery Bill - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
Ban surveillance pricing on groceries. Chow will bring a by-law to the first Council meeting of the new term to prohibit grocers from using shoppers’ personal information to set individualized prices.

-

Cut taxes for independent and community grocery stores. Chow will work with the Province to establish a property tax discount for independent and community grocers, helping neighbourhood businesses compete with the big chains.

-

Help open more community grocery stores. Chow will help connect community grocers with vacant storefronts on Toronto’s main streets, through the City’s economic development department.

-

Fight laws that stop competition. Chow will work with the Province to end Restrictive Covenants that prevent competing grocers from opening in big chains’ plazas or former locations.

The plan builds on Chow’s work saving families on grocers by expanding the school food programs, and her commitment to deliver universal school lunches.

Chow said affordability is a clear choice in this election.

ST. JAMES TOWN (October 23, 2026) - Olivia Chow spoke with families in St. James Town about her vision for a Toronto that’s more caring, affordable and safer. She stood outside the rental building where she grew up, in the neighbourhood that shaped her principled decades-long career standing up for the people of our city.

“My mother worked as a hotel maid. She earned enough to pay the rent and put food on the table here in St. James Town. It wasn't easy, but the City worked for us. I won’t stop fighting until it works for you too,” said Chow. “People deserve a mayor who has their back. I have a plan to bring your costs down, to make our neighbourhoods more safe, to stand up for people and our city no matter what challenges we face.”

Chow shared her perspective from her years of public service, as a school trustee, metro councillor, Toronto city councillor, a member of parliament and now as mayor.
doc_title: Olivia Chow’s Vision for a More Caring, Affordable and Safer City - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
“I've seen entire generations of kids grow up in our city. I’ve seen new communities sprout up. New neighbourhoods begin to shine. Our skyline fill out. I know the decisions we make today will shape the city our children and grandchildren inherit," said Chow.

“This election is a choice. Do we keep moving forward, together, to make life more affordable? Or do we go backwards? Backwards to TTC cuts and higher fares. Backwards to giving away control of our water. Backwards to giveaways for the few, and cuts for everyone else,” said Chow. “I have made my choice. I will keep standing up for families across our city, keep us moving forwards, and keep building a more caring, more affordable and safer city.”

OLIVIA CHOW'S FULL SPEECH - Check against delivery

We often say in our city “Home is Toronto.” Well, behind us here is my first home in Toronto.

I came here when I was 13 years old. And right here, in St. James Town, my family found an affordable apartment. My father struggled with mental illness and could not work. But my mother worked as a hotel maid. She earned enough to pay the rent. Put food on the table. And give us a home.
doc_title: Olivia Chow’s Vision for a More Caring, Affordable and Safer City - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
It wasn't easy. But Toronto was a place where second chances could happen and new lives could be made. A place where an immigrant kid from St. James Town could grow up to become your mayor. And I've never forgotten that.

Because I know firsthand how much it can mean, when someone in a position to make a difference, truly cares what happens to you.

I've spent my life standing up for the people of Toronto. As a school trustee. A metro councillor. A Toronto councillor. A member of parliament. And now, as your mayor.

I've seen entire generations of kids grow up in our city. I’ve seen new communities sprout up. New neighbourhoods begin to shine. Our skyline fill out. Teams win championships, and teams wait for their time to shine again.

And I’ve learned that the decisions we make today will shape the city our children and grandchildren inherit.

Our city has changed a lot. But in all the important ways, I have not.

I’m still the kid from St James Town who is in awe of our city and love for its people, and who has dedicated herself to helping others, to lifting people up, and listening.
doc_title: Olivia Chow’s Vision for a More Caring, Affordable and Safer City - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
That's the kind of mayor I've always tried to be. Never perfect but always focused on the greater good. And that's behind my vision for Toronto.

A more caring, more affordable and safer city. Where everyone belongs.

These are not easy times. When I meet you on the street, I hear the same worries my family had, right here. I know you feel it when you tap your PRESTO card. When you buy groceries. When the rent comes due. When you’re stuck in traffic. These costs come every day. Every week. Every month. And you deserve a mayor who has your back, and who has a plan to bring those costs down.

I have that plan.

Lower transit fares. Lower grocery costs. More homes you can afford.

Under my plan, after 10 TTC rides in a week, the rest are free. Faster, cheaper and safer TTC.

More affordable local grocery stores. More competition. And stopping price gouging.

Feeding more kids in schools. More free children's programs in our libraries.

Helping seniors stay in the homes they love as they age.

15,000 homes under construction. Thousands of them affordable. And I'll build more.
doc_title: Olivia Chow’s Vision for a More Caring, Affordable and Safer City - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
Protecting renters. Cracking down on bad landlords. Making sure apartments are repaired. Because a home should be a place of security. And a caring city must also be a safe city. We've added more than 1,000 police officers and crisis workers. 911 response is twice as fast.

And we're not done. I'll keep investing in safer neighbourhoods. Supporting young people. And protecting the people we love. And I’ll never privatize our water. Never.

That's what caring looks like. Understanding what families are going through. And doing something about it.

This neighbourhood was where I fell in love with Toronto and where I decided to make a difference. And everything I am I owe to my mother, who believed in Toronto. Because Toronto gave her every reason to. Our city worked for us. Which is why I won't stop fighting until it works for you too.

So this election is a simple choice: Do we keep moving forward, together, to make life more affordable?
doc_title: Olivia Chow’s Vision for a More Caring, Affordable and Safer City - Olivia Chow for Mayor of Toronto

text:
Or do we go backwards? Backwards to TTC cuts and higher fares. Backwards to giving away control of our water. Backwards to giveaways for the few, and cuts for everyone else. Why risk it? That’s not what Toronto wants. And it’s what I’ve fought against every day of my life in public service.

So, I have made my choice. I will keep standing up for families across our city. And I will keep bringing costs down.

This race is close. Your vote will decide it. Our city depends on it. So please, vote on Monday, October 26. Bring a friend. Bring a neighbour. And when you do, remember there are two Chows on the ballot, and if you want to keep making progress, it's me, Olivia Chow, number nine.

Let's keep moving forward, together. For a more caring, affordable and safer city.
